t.abric de seguili@38.8,0.0:
The Vall de Pop, or Jalón valley as many foreign residents call it, is a sheltered valley in the north of Alicante province, a few kilometres inland from the coast at Dénia and Xàbia. It is a landscape of vineyards, almond and olive groves and orange trees, with white villages and the mountains rising on all sides. Alcalalí is one of these villages, with a medieval tower in its centre, and Parcent and Orba are nearby. The Abric de Seguilí lies in the hills just outside Alcalalí.

The mountains of the Marina Alta hold many painted shelters, with Levantine, schematic and Macro-schematic art, part of the UNESCO-listed group. The Abric de Seguilí is one of these, a small, protected site in the hills. The art in this area was painted by hunting and later farming communities over thousands of years, and the shelters are often in spectacular places, with views over the valleys.

The Vall de Pop has a long tradition of grape growing, and its Moscatel grapes were once dried to make raisins, which were exported in large quantities through the port of Dénia in the nineteenth century. The valley still produces wine, and the local cooperatives sell it. Jalón has a famous Saturday market, the rastro, which draws crowds from the coast.

The riding around Alcalalí is excellent. The road from Parcent up the Coll de Rates, a mountain pass with a sequence of hairpins and views over the valley and the coast, is famous among professional cyclists, who train here in winter, so expect to share it with them. The roads over the mountains toward Castell de Castells, Tàrbena and the Vall de Laguar are narrow and twisty, with spectacular views. The road from Alcalalí to Llíber and the Vall de Pop is gentler. The surfaces are mostly good.

Alcalalí and Parcent have bars and restaurants, and Pedreguer, about eight kilometres away, is the nearest town with fuel and all services. Local food includes the rice dishes of the area, the coca, and the wines and raisins of the valley. Spring, with almond blossom in late winter, and autumn are the best seasons.
t.pinos@38.7,0.0:
Inland from the busy coast of the Marina Alta, behind Benissa and Calp, the land folds into a series of steep, terraced valleys where almond and olive trees cling to dry-stone walls and white farmhouses sit among the pines. Pinós is a rural area in the hills near Benissa, Senija and Jalón, and the rides link it to the rock-art shelters of the barrancs, the ravines that cut through the limestone of this region, part of the UNESCO listing of Mediterranean prehistoric art. The exact contents of the nearby shelters are for specialists, but the landscape itself has a quiet, timeless beauty, especially in the soft light of late afternoon.

The Jalón valley, just to the west, is known for its vineyards producing sweet moscatel wine and raisins, and in late January and February the almond blossom turns the valley pink and white. Jalón has a large Saturday flea market, and the local bodegas sell wine straight from the barrel. Benissa, about four kilometres away, has a well-preserved old town with a neo-Gothic church locals call the cathedral of the Marina, and its own stretch of rocky coves.

The riding is a highlight: the roads from Benissa through the hills to Jalón, Alcalalí and Parcent, and up to the Coll de Rates pass with its views over the valleys to the sea, are some of the best on the Costa Blanca, with tight bends, steep sections and very little traffic outside the weekends, when cyclists in large groups come out in force, as the Coll de Rates is a favourite training climb for professional teams in winter. Surfaces are generally good, though gravel and dust gather on the corners, and the coastal N-332 is busy, especially in summer. Winter is mild and sunny, and the best season for riding; summer can be very hot.

Benissa has fuel, supermarkets and restaurants, and the coast has endless options for food and accommodation, though prices are higher in the tourist centres. Inland, village restaurants serve hearty dishes like arroz al horno, oven-baked rice with pork, chickpeas and blood sausage, and putxero, a stew of meat and vegetables. A glass of moscatel with almonds after a ride in the hills is a fine local tradition.
t.coves santes de dalt@38.8,0.2:
The Montgó is the great limestone hulk that rises between Dénia and Jávea on the Costa Blanca, a mountain that looks like a sleeping elephant from some angles and dominates every view along this stretch of coast. On its flanks, in shelters and small caves, are prehistoric paintings, and the Coves Santes de Dalt, the upper holy caves, are among the sites in the area recorded as part of the UNESCO Rock Art of the Mediterranean Basin. The paintings here are mostly schematic, simpler and more abstract than the hunting scenes found inland, and the shelters are protected, so viewing usually needs a guided visit.

The Montgó Natural Park surrounds the mountain, with trails through dwarf palms, rosemary, lavender and pine, and on clear days the summit view stretches as far as Ibiza. At the eastern end, the Cabo de San Antonio drops sheer into the sea, with a lighthouse and a viewpoint over Jávea's bay that is particularly beautiful at sunset.

Jávea, three kilometres away, is a town of thirty thousand that swells enormously in summer, with a large foreign community, an old town of white houses and Gothic church, a fishing port and a beach promenade. Dénia, nine kilometres off, is bigger, with a castle above the port and ferries to the Balearics, and it is famous for its red prawns. Fuel and food are no problem.

For riding, the coast roads are busy in high season and full of roundabouts, but the hills behind are wonderful. The roads inland toward the Vall de Laguar, Vall d'Ebo and Castell de Castells are tight, twisty and often almost empty, climbing through terraced almond and olive groves into dramatic limestone country. Come in spring, when the almond blossom is over but the hills are green and fragrant, or in autumn, when the crowds have gone and the sea is still warm enough for a swim after a morning in the mountains.
t.cova del mig dia@38.8,0.1:
The Montgó dominates the coast between Dénia and Xàbia, a massive limestone mountain rising to 753 metres straight from the sea, its profile said to resemble a sleeping elephant. The Cova del Mig Dia, the cave of midday, is in the flanks of the Montgó, one of several caves and shelters on the mountain, some with traces of prehistoric occupation and rock art. The Montgó is a natural park, with paths leading through scrub and pine to caves, viewpoints and the summit.

The mountain is a refuge for plants and wildlife in a coastline heavily developed for tourism. The Cap de Sant Antoni, at its eastern end, is a marine reserve, with cliffs dropping into clear water. Dénia, on the northern side, has a castle on a hill above the port, from which ferries sail to the Balearic Islands. Xàbia, to the south, has a historic centre and a beautiful bay. Both towns are popular with foreign residents and tourists, and the coast between them is lined with villas.

The riding around the Montgó is short but scenic. The road from Dénia to Xàbia passes around the western side of the mountain, and the road to the Cap de Sant Antoni lighthouse offers views over the bay of Xàbia and the cliffs. The coastal road south of Dénia, to Les Rotes, is narrow and winding, with views of rocky coves. Traffic can be heavy in summer, especially in the towns. Inland, the mountains of the Marina Alta, around the valleys of Laguar and Gallinera, offer some of the best riding in the region, with tight bends and spectacular views.

Dénia and Xàbia are both towns of over thirty thousand, with fuel, shops and restaurants. Dénia is famous for its red prawns, the gamba roja, considered among the best in Spain, and both towns have excellent seafood restaurants. Gata de Gorgos, nearby, is known for its basketry and crafts. A walk on the Montgó in the early morning, before the heat, gives views over the coast and, on very clear days, all the way to Ibiza.
t.penya del vicari@38.7,0.0:
On a map of the Costa Blanca, the Serra de Bernia looks like a wall dropped between two very different worlds. On one side, high-rise Benidorm and the busy coast; on the other, the quiet valleys of Jalón and Guadalest. The Penya del Vicari is one of the rocky outcrops in these hills above Altea and Calp, a place where the limestone is cut by caves and shelters, some of which carry traces of prehistoric painting. It is a small, quiet site in an area otherwise famous for sun loungers.

Altea is the nearest town, and it is a pleasant surprise: an old village of whitewashed houses climbing to a church with blue-tiled domes, with a long seafront below. Calp, to the north, is dominated by the Penyal d'Ifac, a sheer rock rising from the sea that is now a nature reserve, home to peregrine falcons and seabirds. Between them, the Bernia ridge carries the ruins of a sixteenth-century fortress built under Philip II to watch the coast and the Morisco population of the valleys, later destroyed on royal orders. A walking trail circles the ridge and passes through a natural tunnel in the rock, the Forat.

The riding here is a game of contrasts. The coast road between Altea and Calp is busy and slow, with roundabouts and traffic lights, but turn inland and the roads become narrow, steep and twisting, climbing through almond terraces and pine woods with views that sweep down to the sea. The lane up to the Bernia area and the roads through Bolulla and Tàrbena are particularly good, with plenty of hairpins and a lot of elevation in a few kilometres. Watch for cyclists, goats and the occasional rental car taking the bend in the middle.

Fuel, cafés and everything else are easy in Altea and Calp. The coast is known for rice dishes and seafood, and a lunch on a terrace above the harbour is hard to argue with. In summer, the heat and crowds make early morning or evening the best times to ride; in winter, the climate is mild and the light is wonderful, which is why the cycling teams come. If you head out to the shelters, check access and wear decent shoes. And make time for a moment at a viewpoint above Altea, with the blue domes below, the Penyal d'Ifac on the horizon and the Mediterranean behaving like a postcard.
t.yongling tomb of the qing dynasty@41.3,1:
Before Beijing, before the Forbidden City, the people who would rule China as the Qing dynasty were a clan of forest-edge farmers and hunters in the hills of eastern Liaoning. Yongling is their ancestral grave. It lies near Xinbin, a Manchu autonomous county in the mountains east of Fushun, not far from Hetu Ala, the small hill town that Nurhaci made his first capital, and it holds the remains of the forebears of that remarkable man, who united the Jurchen tribes in the late sixteenth century and set in motion the conquest of China by his successors.

The tomb complex was laid out in the Chinese imperial manner, but with Manchu touches. Walls, gates, halls and spirit-way run along a hillside, with tiled roofs in yellow and green, and from the upper terrace you look out over a quiet green valley with the Suzi river below. It is smaller and more intimate than the Ming and Qing imperial tombs near Beijing, and it is part of the same World Heritage listing, the Imperial Tombs of the Ming and Qing Dynasties. Nearby, Wunu Mountain City, a mountain fortress of the Goguryeo kingdom, tells of an even older people who held these hills two thousand years ago.

The countryside is the real reason to come. Eastern Liaoning is hilly, wooded and surprisingly green, with oak, pine and larch on the slopes and terraced fields of maize and soybean in the valleys, and the villages are low, brick and tile. Autumn is outstanding, when the forests turn orange and red, while summer is warm and wet and winter is bitterly cold with snow on the ground for months.

Riding a foreign motorbike in China is complicated, since it generally requires a Chinese licence, local plates and registration, and often a guide, so most visitors come by car with a driver or by public bus from Fushun or Shenyang. Fuel and food are easy in Xinbin and the larger towns, and local Manchu cooking features dumplings, pickled cabbage and stews. Check opening times in advance, and allow plenty of time, since the roads are often slow and sometimes busy with trucks.
t.santa barbara@34.4,-119.7:
The Pacific Coast Highway has a way of ending in places that look like film sets, and Santa Barbara is the best of them. The city sits on a narrow shelf of land between the Santa Ynez Mountains and the ocean, facing south, which is unusual on the Californian coast, so the sun seems to hang over the water in the afternoon. The red tile roofs, white stucco walls and arched arcades are not an accident. After an earthquake in 1925 destroyed much of downtown, the city rebuilt in a unified Spanish Colonial Revival style, and the result is a place that feels more like Andalusia than Los Angeles.

The history runs deeper than the architecture. The Chumash people lived on this coast for thousands of years, and in 1786 the Spanish founded Mission Santa Barbara, which they called the Queen of the Missions, on a hill above the town. Its twin bell towers and rose-pink facade are among the most photographed sights in California, and the mission is still an active church. In the town centre stands the county courthouse, built in 1929 with a clock tower you can climb for a free view over the roofs and the harbour, and nearby Stearns Wharf, which dates from the 1870s, reaches out into the bay.

For riders, the approach on Highway 101 along the coast from the south is mostly a fast, straightforward road, with the ocean on one side and the mountains on the other, and the section north of Ventura is among the prettiest. The real riding begins when you leave the coast. San Marcos Pass, on Highway 154, climbs into the mountains behind the city with sweeping bends, and it leads to the Santa Ynez Valley, where vineyards and small towns made the film Sideways famous. Morning fog, known as the marine layer, can linger until midday in late spring and early summer, so the best weather is often in the afternoon or in autumn.

There is no shortage of fuel, food or hotels in a city of some ninety thousand people, though prices are high, and parking along State Street is easy to find in garages. Try fish tacos at a harbourside stand, or a glass of local pinot noir. Watch for cyclists, who are everywhere, and for the speed limits, which are strictly enforced.
t.coves santes de baix@38.8,0.2:
The Montgó is the mountain that defines this coast, a great limestone whale of a massif, 753 metres high, standing between Dénia and Xàbia and visible from far out at sea. It is a natural park, with rare plants, Mediterranean scrub and cliffs where birds of prey nest, and its profile is the one that sailors used for centuries as a landmark. Xàbia, known to English speakers as Jávea, lies at its foot, a town of about 30,000 people in three parts: a walled old town on a hill, a harbour district, and a long arc of beach, the Arenal.

The old town is worth time. Its fortified Gothic church of San Bartolomé, built with battlements and thick walls to resist pirate raids, dominates the narrow lanes, and a market hall and a handful of old gates survive. Xàbia was a centre for the Moscatel grape and for raisin production, and the wine and the dried fruit have a long history, with vineyards on the slopes of the Montgó still producing sweet wines. The coast has dramatic capes: the Cap de la Nau, the easternmost point of the province, and the Cap de Sant Antoni, with cliffs and small coves.

The Coves Santes, the holy caves, are in the cliffs of this coast, and the name suggests that the site has long been special to local people. Caves and shelters in the area have yielded prehistoric finds, and the region is part of the larger Valencian world of Levantine painted rock, listed by UNESCO in 1998. Access to such places is limited, so ask at the tourist office in Xàbia about what is open and what is not.

For a rider, the coast is a pleasure in the off-season and a trial in high summer. The roads along the cliffs have bends and good views, but the traffic in July and August is very heavy, and parking near the beaches is hard. Early morning and the shoulder months, April to June and September to October, are better. Fuel stations are easy to find in Xàbia and Dénia. Try arroz a banda or the red prawns of Dénia, which are among the best in Spain, and the local sweet Moscatel with a dessert.
t.c7 south east area mao@39.9,4.2:
Menorca is the quieter of the Balearic islands, and Maó, at the eastern end, is its capital and main port. It sits on one of the longest natural harbours in the Mediterranean, a deep inlet that has been fought over by Britons, French and Spanish and that has left the town with Georgian sash windows next to Catalan balconies. The island itself is a UNESCO biosphere reserve, and the south-east, around Maó and Sant Lluís, is where its prehistoric remains are most thickly spread.

Menorca's prehistoric builders left behind talayots, large stone towers, and taulas, T-shaped standing stones, which are found nowhere else in quite this form. The monuments belong to a culture that lasted from the Bronze Age through to Roman times, and they are scattered through fields and scrub, often with a stone wall running round them. Trepucó, close to Maó, is among the most accessible of the sites, and Torre d'en Galmés, a little farther west, is the largest. This stretch of the south-east is dotted with them.

The riding is gentle and unhurried. The main road across the island, the Me-1, runs from Maó through Alaior and Ferreries to Ciutadella, and the side roads from it to the south coast are narrow, bordered by drystone walls and low pines, with sharp little bends where they meet the cala beaches. Speed limits are low and enforced, and in July and August the roads fill with hire cars and scooters. The pleasant months are May, June and late September, when the island is warm and quiet.

Maó, with around twenty-nine thousand people, has all the fuel and shops you could need, and Sant Lluís is a pretty whitewashed town with a few good bars. Locals will tell you that mayonnaise was born here, as mahonesa, and that the island's gin, flavoured with juniper and distilled in old copper stills, is a good drink in the evening. Whether or not the mayonnaise story is true, both are on the table at lunch in the harbour.
t.c2 southwest area@39.9,3.9:
Ciutadella is the old capital of Menorca, a handsome town of nearly thirty thousand people at the western end of the island, with a small harbour lined with fish restaurants and a cathedral built on the site of a mosque. The south-west corner of the island, below the town, holds some of the finest prehistoric remains on Menorca, including the burial chamber known as the Naveta des Tudons, a stone structure shaped like an upturned boat that is among the oldest roofed buildings in Europe. It belongs to the talayotic culture that built towers and T-shaped sanctuaries across the island over many centuries.

The island's quietest beaches are here, too. Cala Turqueta, Macarella and Macarelleta sit at the end of short roads through pine woods, and the water in them is a pale turquoise that looks Caribbean on a sunny day. Access in summer is restricted by car parks that fill early, so arrive in the morning or in the evening, or come outside the high season.

Riding on Menorca is mellow. The road from Maó to Ciutadella runs straight and quiet across the middle of the island, and the side roads that fork south to the beaches are narrow, lined with the dry stone walls that the island is known for. Speed limits are low, enforcement is real, and in high summer the roads fill with rental cars. A motorbike is a good way to get about, and parking at the beaches is easier. Cala Galdana, in the municipality of Ferreries, sits in a deep cleft between pine-clad cliffs and has a tourist village of the sort you'd expect.

Ciutadella has fuel and good places to eat. A grilled fish or a lobster stew, the caldereta, is the local treat, and the pomada, a mix of gin and lemonade, is the drink at every festival. In June the Sant Joan festival fills the streets with horses and riders, an astonishing sight.

Come in May, June or September for the best combination of warmth and space. Winter is mild but windy, and the north wind, the tramontana, can be strong.
t.banff@51.2,-115.6:
Banff in the morning has a particular feel: cold air coming off the glacier-fed Bow River, mist clinging to Mount Rundle, and the smell of pine and woodsmoke from kitchens. The town sits in the heart of the Canadian Rockies at about 1,400 metres, hemmed in by peaks, and it exists because of hot springs. In the 1880s railway workers found warm water at Cave and Basin, and the government made the area a reserve that grew into Canada's first national park.

Today Banff is a resort town, busy and polished, and it handles tourists very well. Shops, restaurants and hotels crowd the main street, Banff Avenue, with views straight down to Cascade Mountain. The Banff Springs Hotel, a castle-like structure built by the Canadian Pacific Railway, overlooks the valley. Wildlife wanders freely: elk graze on lawns, and bighorn sheep, black bears and sometimes grizzlies appear along the roads, so take warnings seriously.

For riders, the real prize is the Bow Valley Parkway, the quieter older road to Lake Louise that runs parallel to the main highway. It has a low speed limit, wide views and a good chance of seeing animals at dawn or dusk. Parts of it close seasonally to protect wildlife, so check before heading out. A park pass is required for stops in the national park. Weather in the Rockies can change by the hour, with snow possible even in early summer, so carry warm layers and waterproofs. The best months are late June to September.

Banff has fuel, supermarkets and every sort of restaurant, though prices are high and summer weekends are crowded. Canmore, eighteen kilometres east, is a larger place with a more local feel and often cheaper options. The hot springs on the hillside are there for tired legs, and book rooms months ahead in summer.
t.hualien@24.0,121.6:
Hualien lies on Taiwan's wild east coast, squeezed between the Pacific and a wall of mountains that rise to over three thousand metres within a few dozen kilometres of the sea. The city is relaxed, with a lively night market, sea-view cafes and the slightly weathered air of a place that is regularly shaken by earthquakes and typhoons. It is also the gateway to Taroko Gorge, where the Liwu river has cut a deep canyon through marble.

The road that follows the gorge, the Central Cross-Island Highway, is one of the great feats of Taiwanese engineering. It was built between 1956 and 1960 by army veterans and other workers, mostly with hand tools, across steep marble cliffs, and a number of men lost their lives during the work. Roadside shrines remember them, and the Eternal Spring Shrine, built over a waterfall, commemorates the dead. Today the road passes tunnels, narrow ledges and bridges, with the river shimmering turquoise far below.

Riding it is exciting and demanding. Bends are tight, and the road is narrow, with marble walls on one side and sheer drops on the other. Rockfall is a real hazard, tour buses take the corners wide, and the tunnels are dark. Sections of the highway are often closed after earthquakes or typhoons, as happened after the strong quake in April 2024, so always check current road status and any permit requirements before setting out. The weather turns misty and cold at higher altitudes, so bring layers. Spring and autumn offer the clearest skies; summer is hot and humid, with a typhoon season to watch.

Hualien city has fuel, workshops, hotels and endless food stalls, so prepare there. Along the highway, supplies are limited, and it is wise to carry water and snacks. Try the local mochi and the sweet peanut-powdered rice cakes, and a plate of fresh seafood at the night market. The indigenous Truku people, who have lived in the gorge area for centuries, are part of the area's culture, and visiting local craft shops is a good way to support them.
t.sanxiantai@23.1,121.4:
Sanxiantai means Terrace of the Three Immortals, and the name comes from a legend of three Taoist immortals who are said to have rested on the offshore island here. It lies on Taiwan's east coast, near the town of Chenggong, where the sea turns a startling deep blue, and a long arched footbridge, shaped like a dragon's back, runs out to the island across a lagoon. Seen from the shore, with the waves breaking on dark volcanic rock, it has a wild, sculptural look.

The coast here is the homeland of the Amis, one of Taiwan's indigenous peoples, whose festivals, with dance and song in bright costume, are held in summer and are among the most colourful events on the island. The nearby fishing harbour at Chenggong is known for catching marlin and swordfish, and fish markets and seafood restaurants sell the catch. The sea off this coast is deep and swept by the Kuroshio Current, a warm Pacific stream that carries marine life north.

The Provincial Highway 11 is one of Taiwan's most beautiful roads. It hugs the shoreline with the mountains behind, and on clear days the road is quiet, with slow curves, sea views and little traffic. Fishing villages, rice fields and roadside stalls selling pineapples and sugar apples appear along the way. Typhoons from July to October can damage roads and bring heavy rain, and in winter the northeast monsoon can make the coast windy and damp. Spring and autumn are gentle seasons, and the light at dawn, when the sun rises out of the Pacific, is superb.

The island is a mix of rugged rock and sandy patches, ideal for walking, snorkelling and sitting on the rocks with a drink. Facilities on site are simple, with a car park, a few stalls and toilets. For fuel and a proper meal, head to Chenggong or the larger city of Taitung to the south, and carry water on hot days. Rain gear is useful all year.
t.dulan@22.9,121.2:
Dulan sits on Taiwan's east coast, where the mountains drop almost straight into the Pacific. The village, in Taitung County about fifteen kilometres north of Taitung City, lies along Provincial Highway 11, a ribbon of road that runs between the Coastal Mountain Range and the sea, and the combination of mountain, surf and open sky has made it a haven for surfers, artists and refugees from the island's crowded west.

The people who lived here first were the Amis and other Indigenous communities, and their culture is still alive in the villages along the coast, with harvest festivals, songs and a tradition of weaving and wood carving. In Dulan, an old sugar factory has been turned into a creative hub, with galleries, workshops and a café where musicians play on weekends. The hills behind the village hold sacred places for the local communities, and Dulan Mountain, as the ridge is called, rises sharply above the road.

Highway 11 is one of the great coastal rides of Asia. The road follows the shoreline with views of the ocean on one side and green hills on the other, passing fishing harbours, rock formations and small beaches. Surfaces are generally excellent and traffic is light, although in holiday weekends scooters and tourist buses crowd the coast. Typhoons between July and October can close sections of the road with landslides and wave damage, so check the news before you set out. The wind from the sea can be fierce. Taiwan drives on the right, helmets are mandatory, and speed cameras are common, so keep to the limits.

Fuel is easy in Taitung, and there are stations along the coast, although they are spaced widely in places, so fill up before leaving. In Dulan itself you will find cafés, noodle shops and small convenience stores, which are open all hours. Fresh fish, grilled squid and pork rice are standard fare, and the local millet wine is strong.

Time your ride for the early morning, when the Pacific is calm and the sunrise comes up over the water.
t.los angeles@34.1,-118.2:
Route 66 does not end in a blaze of glory. After more than three thousand kilometres from Chicago, the old highway frays into the boulevards of Los Angeles, and its last stretch is a patchwork of Foothill Boulevard, Colorado Boulevard and Santa Monica Boulevard, ending officially at the pier in Santa Monica, with the Pacific beyond. The point on the map here is the old centre, where the city began in 1781 as a Spanish pueblo, and a few blocks of adobe buildings and a Mexican market street, Olvera Street, are still standing, near the grand Spanish-style Union Station, which opened in 1939.

The city is a sprawl of neighbourhoods more than a single place, joined by freeways that carry some of the heaviest traffic in the United States. Hollywood, Griffith Park and its observatory, the beaches of Santa Monica and Venice, and the downtown skyscrapers are all within an hour or so of one another, depending on the hour. The Arroyo Seco Parkway to Pasadena, opened in 1940, was the first freeway in the western United States, and its tight curves and short ramps look quaint beside later designs.

For a motorcyclist, LA has a particular pleasure and a particular hazard. California allows lane splitting, riding between lines of slow traffic, under guidance from the highway patrol that advises doing so at a modest speed difference, and it turns an hour of gridlock into a manageable commute. It also means drivers are used to bikes appearing between cars, though not all are careful. Rush hours are long and heavy, with mornings and late afternoons the worst, so plan to arrive and leave at off-peak times. Fuel is available everywhere, though prices are higher than in most states.

The weather is warm and mostly dry, with a marine layer of cloud on the coast in late spring and early summer, locals call it May Gray and June Gloom, and the hot, dry Santa Ana winds in autumn. Smog can be heavy in summer. The best way to end the Route 66 journey is a slow cruise west along Santa Monica Boulevard to the pier, watching the light turn orange, and then a late dinner by the water.
t.algiers@36.8,3.1:
Algiers climbs a hillside above the Mediterranean in a white amphitheatre, which is why it is called Algiers the White. The old quarter, the Casbah, is a maze of narrow lanes, stairways and blind alleys that drop steeply toward the sea, with houses leaning over the paths so closely that the sunlight hardly reaches the ground. UNESCO listed it in 1992 as an example of a North African Islamic city, with an Ottoman citadel, old mosques and palaces. Many of the buildings are in bad repair, and there is a long-running effort to save them, but the life of the quarter goes on, with children playing football in the lanes and cats on every wall.

Below the Casbah lie the French colonial streets, with arcaded boulevards, grand post office and long seafront terraces, built in the nineteenth and early twentieth centuries. Algeria was part of France for a hundred and thirty years, and the architecture shows it, while the memory of the war of independence between 1954 and 1962 colours the modern history. Above, on a hill, stands the basilica of Notre-Dame d'Afrique, looking over the bay, and on another hill a vast concrete monument to the martyrs of the war rises like three palm leaves. The botanical garden at Hamma is a quiet place with giant trees and long avenues.

Riding in and out of Algiers takes confidence. The traffic is dense and fast, signals are optional, and road quality varies, with potholes and sudden changes of surface. Leaving the city to the west brings you along the coast toward Tipasa, with the Chenoua mountain rising ahead and the sea glittering below, and the road runs through villages and between fields of citrus and vines. There are police checkpoints on many roads, so carry your passport, vehicle papers and insurance, and check your country's current travel advice before you go.

Fuel is cheap, with stations on all the main roads, though queues can occur. Food is a pleasure, with couscous on Fridays, grilled fish on the coast, and mint tea and pastries in the cafés. The best seasons are spring and autumn. Summers are hot and humid, and winters bring rain and chilly winds. In the evening, the whole city comes out to walk along the seafront, and the sound of conversation is as constant as the sea.
t.tipasa parc archaeologique est@36.6,2.5:
Albert Camus came to Tipasa as a young man and wrote about it in an essay called Nuptials at Tipasa, which describes the wild thyme, the sun on the ruins and the sea as a kind of marriage between a person and the world. He wrote that in spring, Tipasa is inhabited by the gods and the gods speak in the sun and the scent of absinthe plants. Anyone who has walked here on a bright day in April will know what he meant.
