t.hehuanshan high road@24.1,121.3:
Wuling, the pass just beyond the Hehuanshan high road, is the highest paved road crossing in East Asia, at 3,275 metres, and the ride there from the lowlands is a journey through half the climates of the world. In Puli the air is warm and smells of fruit and betel nut, and by the time you reach the pass you are in a landscape of alpine meadow, bamboo grass and wind-sculpted fir, with temperatures that can hover near freezing even in summer. The road is Provincial Highway 14A, a spur off the main east-west highway, and it climbs from the valley of Puli in a long succession of curves for more than eighty kilometres.

The surface is generally good, the bends are long and open, and in places the road clings to the edge of the mountain with sheer drops on one side. Cloud can come down suddenly, and a clear morning may turn into a rainy afternoon. Winter brings snow and ice to the highest sections, and the road is sometimes closed, so check conditions before setting out. Typhoons and landslides can also cut the road, and repairs are common. Wear layers and bring rain gear, as the temperature at the top can be some twenty degrees colder than at Puli.

Hehuanshan itself is a cluster of peaks, the highest at more than 3,400 metres, covered in bamboo grass that turns gold in autumn, with views across a sea of cloud to the central mountain ridge. Taiwan is a young, quickly rising island, with some of the steepest relief in the world, and it shows here. The road you are on is part of the Central Cross-Island Highway system, which was built in the 1950s by thousands of retired soldiers working with hand tools, and many lost their lives in the process. Beyond Wuling the road descends east toward the Taroko Gorge and the coast.

Fuel is available in Puli and in the villages on the western side, but there is little at the top, so fill the tank beforehand. A small shop near the summit sells hot drinks and snacks. Thin air at this altitude can cause headaches and dizziness, and engines run a little rough, so go steadily. The best seasons are autumn and spring, when the weather is clear and the temperature bearable. At dawn the light on the peaks is among the most beautiful you will see.
t.qixingtan beach@24.0,121.6:
Taiwan's east coast does not have sand beaches in the postcard sense. Qixingtan, whose name means Seven Star Lake, is a long curve of grey pebbles on the Pacific side of Hualien, where the water goes from shallow to deep in a few steps and the waves arrive with real weight. Swimming is discouraged because of the undertow, and signs make that clear, but sitting on the stones with a drink while the sea rolls in is a very good way to end a ride. Behind you the Central Range rises almost straight from the coast, with cloud caught in the ridges, and on a clear morning the sun comes up out of the ocean in front of you.

The coast road here, Provincial Highway 11, runs south from Hualien through fishing villages, rice paddies, rocky headlands and long, easy bends with the ocean on one side. The surface is generally well kept, traffic is moderate, and there are plenty of viewpoints and small cafes. Scooters are everywhere, and Taiwanese drivers tend to overtake in ways that require attention, so keep your speed relaxed and watch the mirrors. It is a ride for taking slowly, with the smell of salt and wet stone in the air.

This is also the doorstep of Taroko Gorge, where the Liwu river has cut a deep marble canyon into the mountains to the north-west. The cliff road along the gorge is dramatic, but it has been closed repeatedly after earthquakes and rockfall, including after the strong earthquake of April 2024, so always check road and permit status before riding up. The area around Hualien is one of the most seismically active in Taiwan, and the local people take it calmly.

Hualien City has more than 350,000 people, so fuel, bike shops and hotels are easy, and the night market is the place to try local dishes such as wonton soup and sticky rice with peanuts. The best months for riding are October to May, with cooler weather and fewer crowds, while typhoons can hit between July and October and shut roads for days.
t.big@33.8,-117.9:
Garden Grove sits in the middle of Orange County's great flat basin, a tapestry of low-rise suburbs between Disneyland to the north and the beach towns to the south-west. The label on this stop only says Big, presumably short for Big Bear, so what I can honestly describe is the setting, which is the low, built-up plain from which the long ride into the mountains begins. The San Bernardino range stands to the north-east, and on a clear winter morning its snow-covered ridges seem to float above the haze.

The city has a character of its own. It has one of the largest Vietnamese communities outside Vietnam, centred on nearby Little Saigon in Westminster and Garden Grove, where shopping malls and streets of restaurants sell pho, banh mi and strong iced coffee with condensed milk. Early in the day, the bakeries open with trays of fresh bread, and the smell drifts out to the street. The big glass church that once belonged to a famous televangelist, now a Catholic cathedral, stands on the edge of town, a surprising presence among low buildings.

The riding is simple urban work. Boulevards run in grids with a light at nearly every block, the freeways run fast but crowded, and traffic piles up on weekdays from early morning. Lane splitting is legal in California, but common sense matters. To reach the mountains, riders usually take the freeways east, then climb up Highway 330 or 18 into the San Bernardino range, a transition from sprawl to pine forest in about two hours. Go early, preferably before 7 am, to avoid the worst of the traffic.

Everything you need is here, since the city has about 175,000 people. Fuel stations stand at nearly every junction, and Fountain Valley, to the south, has even more shops. Take a hot drink for the mountain portion, because the air at Big Bear, at about 6,700 feet, is far cooler than in the basin. Spring and autumn offer the most pleasant weather, and Santa Ana wind days in autumn can be hot, dry and gusty.
t.pollenca@39.9,3.0:
Pollença sits in a shallow bowl at the foot of the Serra de Tramuntana, the limestone mountain range that runs down Mallorca's northwest coast, and it is one of the island's best-looking towns. Pale stone houses, green shutters and plane-lined squares fill the old center, and above it rises the Puig de Maria, a hill topped with a small monastery. The town has the confident, slightly arty air of a place that painters have loved for a century, and its main square, the Plaça Major, fills with a market on Sundays.

Two features are almost obligatory. The Calvari, a long stairway of 365 steps lined with cypress trees, climbs to a chapel on a hill, and the climb is cooler at dusk. The Roman Bridge, an old stone arch over a dry stream bed just outside the center, is one of the few reminders that this area was settled in antiquity. In summer the town hosts a festival of classical music in the cloister of a former convent, and the cafes on the square are the place to sit with a coffee and watch.

For riders, Pollença is the northern gateway to Ma-10, the road down the spine of the Tramuntana, which UNESCO declared a World Heritage cultural landscape. It runs south past Lluc Monastery, one of the island's spiritual centers, and on through terraced olive groves, rock walls and high passes, with long views to the sea, and the tarmac is mostly good, with tight bends. The road is hugely popular with cyclists, especially in spring, and with tour buses in high season, so it can be busy and slow, and early morning is the time. At the north end, the road to Cap de Formentor, a narrow ribbon cut into cliffs above the sea, is a classic, though it is crowded in summer.

The town has everything: fuel, supermarkets, banks and restaurants, and Port de Pollença, a short ride away, has a seafront promenade. Alcúdia, the other main town nearby, has an old walled center. The best months are April, May and October, with mild weather and fewer visitors. In summer the heat is fierce by midday and the traffic heavy, while in winter, rain and rockfall can affect mountain roads. Watch for loose gravel on corners and for cyclists on the bends.
t.la canada@34.2,-118.2:
La Cañada Flintridge sits at the foot of the San Gabriel Mountains, in the foothills north of Pasadena, and its main job on a ride is to be the last good place to buy petrol before the road turns serious. This is where the Angeles Crest Highway, State Route 2, begins its climb into the Angeles National Forest, and where a lot of Los Angeles riders meet on a weekend morning. The town itself is a prosperous, leafy suburb of about twenty thousand people, known for its good schools, the Descanso Gardens, a large botanical garden with camellias and a rose garden, and for being the home of NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory, whose engineers have sent spacecraft to every planet from this corner of the valley.

Fill the tank here. The mountain road ahead is long, with limited services, and the climbs burn more fuel than you expect. The highway rises from the suburbs in tight bends, passing through chaparral hillsides that smell of sage and warm dust on hot days, and climbing past viewpoints over the Los Angeles basin. At the higher levels, it enters pine and fir forest, with temperatures dropping noticeably. Beyond Islip Saddle, it continues toward Wrightwood and the high desert, with long views over the Mojave on a clear day.

The road is a classic motorcycle ride, with smooth surface in many places and long, flowing curves, but also a certain risk. Traffic can be heavy on weekends, with riders, cyclists and drivers, and some sections have fatalities every year, so rider caution is a good idea. The highway has also been closed repeatedly by landslides and wildfire. The 2009 Station Fire started in these hills and burned over a hundred and sixty thousand acres, and rock falls after storms remain a threat. Check the Caltrans road status before going, because gates at various points may be shut.

Weather in the foothills is warm and often smoggy in summer, and the mountains can be much cooler, with snow at the upper elevations in winter. A light jacket under your riding gear is useful, and water is worth carrying. Early morning is best, both for traffic and for the light, and spring, after winter rain has turned the hills green, is the finest season of all.

When you return, La Cañada has no shortage of cafes and a few decent places to eat along Foothill Boulevard, and the town makes a pleasant end to a day.
t.calabasas@34.1,-118.7:
Calabasas is the last neat suburb before the Santa Monica Mountains turn wild, and for motorcyclists it is where a Southern California ride begins. The town sits at the western end of the San Fernando Valley, with a tidy main street, gated communities and a strip of shops, and just beyond it the road enters canyon country. The name comes from the Spanish word for pumpkins or gourds, and local stories claim it refers to a wagon that spilled its load or to the wild gourds along the creek.

From here, Las Virgenes Road and Malibu Canyon Road drop south through a steep canyon to Pacific Coast Highway, a quick, winding run past rock walls and, on the side, the Malibu Creek State Park, where the television series M*A*S*H was filmed. The canyon road is famous among riders, with tight curves, blind corners and a long record of accidents, so it demands respect. Mulholland Highway, named for William Mulholland, the engineer who brought Owens Valley water to Los Angeles, winds west along the ridge, twisting through oak woodland and chaparral with views down to the ocean.

At Cornell Road in Agoura Hills, the Rock Store, a roadside cafe and gathering spot, has been a biker hangout for decades, and on Sunday mornings hundreds of motorcycles and cars cluster in the lot. The crowds can be intense, but it is part of the culture of the place, and a good place to meet other riders. Weekends are busy, with cyclists, sports cars and sightseers on the narrow lanes, so weekday mornings are better.

Calabasas has plenty of fuel and food, which is why it makes a good start: top the tank here, because the canyon roads have no stations. The marine layer in late spring and early summer fills the canyons with cool fog until late morning, while autumn offers clear, warm days. Fire and mudslides can close canyon roads, particularly after winter rains, and the road surface is often scattered with gravel and fallen branches. Speeding tickets are common, and police patrol the canyons regularly.
t.escondido@33.1,-117.1:
Escondido is the biggest city in San Diego County's north inland area, a sprawling place of about 150,000 people in a wide valley of avocado and citrus groves, and its job in a ride is to supply everything a rider might need before heading into the hills. The name means hidden in Spanish, which reflects the way the valley sits tucked behind a ridge. The town grew after the railway came in the 1880s, with citrus and grapes as its early industries, and today it is a mixture of breweries, farmland, strip malls and a historic downtown with a good arts centre and a few lively restaurants.

There are fuel stations everywhere, so this is the place to fill up, and to buy water. From here, the road winds east and north into the hills of the Palomar Mountain area, and the real riding begins. State Route 76 follows the San Luis Rey River east toward Pauma Valley, among orchards and rocks, with soft bends and rolling hills. From there, the road to the top of Palomar Mountain climbs through dozens of tight corners, shaded by oak and then by pine, rising to about five thousand feet. It is narrow and twisty, with some rough tar and occasional gravel, so take it slowly, but the views south and west out over the valley are well worth it.

Palomar Mountain is home to the Palomar Observatory, which opened in 1948 with the 200-inch Hale telescope, the largest in the world for decades. You can visit the dome and the small museum, and peer in at one of the great pieces of twentieth-century science. The ridge is also green and wooded, a noticeable contrast with the dry chaparral below, and in winter, snow can fall on top. Check the weather before climbing in colder months. The East Grade Road on the other side of the mountain is steeper and narrower still, a famous test for riders who like their corners tight.

Wildlife includes deer, wild turkeys and coyotes, with the odd mountain lion in the back country. Spring wildflowers and the smell of orange blossom in the valleys are real delights, and the best riding is in the spring or autumn, when the heat of summer has eased. Summer can be extremely hot at the bottom, with temperatures above thirty-five degrees Celsius.

For food, Escondido has everything, from taquerias to craft beer to pizzerias, and the old downtown is the best place to stroll afterward.
t.daxi@24.9,121.3:
Daxi is a small town in the hills of Taoyuan, on the Dahan river, and it marks the start of one of Taiwan's most popular mountain roads. The old street, with arched facades in baroque style built during the Japanese colonial period, runs down toward the river, lined with shops selling dried tofu, a local speciality that Taiwanese people travel for. The tofu is dense, savoury and a little chewy, and you can buy it in many flavours. In the evening the street fills with families and the smell of grilled food.

The town has an unusual historical landmark. Chiang Kai-shek, who led the Nationalists to Taiwan after 1949, was kept in a temporary mausoleum at Daxi after his death in 1975, and the compound, with its gardens and quiet pavilions, is now a place of memory, with statues of the leader that have been gathered here from around the island. It is a strange and stirring place, and a short walk from the old street.

The reason riders come is Provincial Highway 7, the Northern Cross-Island Highway. From Daxi it climbs west to east through the mountains of northern Taiwan, passing Shimen reservoir, the Baling Bridge, and mountain villages with tea and persimmon orchards, before dropping to the Lanyang plain at Yilan. It is a well-known biker's road, with many bends, tunnels, forests of cedar and cypress, and views of cloud wrapping the ridges. The tarmac is generally good but landslides and typhoons can close sections, so check road conditions before you set out. Mist and rain are common, and the temperature drops sharply with altitude.

Daxi is a town of eighty thousand and has plenty of fuel stations and convenience stores. Remember that Taiwan is busy with scooters, that traffic rules are loosely observed, and that heavy bikes are common on weekends on the mountain highways. Spring and autumn offer the clearest views.
t.yilan@24.8,121.8:
Yilan lies on the Pacific coast in north-eastern Taiwan, in the Lanyang plain, a green triangle of rice paddies and scallion fields that is hemmed in by steep mountains on three sides and the open ocean on the fourth. It is wetter than the rest of the island, with rain in most months, and the damp gives the landscape a soft, mossy look. Offshore, Guishan Island, shaped like a turtle, rises from the water and can be seen from the shore on a clear day, and boats go out for whale and dolphin watching from the harbour at Wushih.

The county is known for food and hot springs. The Sanxing scallions are famed across the island, and street stalls sell them wrapped in pancakes. The night markets of Luodong, with their grilled meats, sweet snacks and local specialities, are a highlight. At Jiaoxi, a spa town nearby, hot water springs are piped into hotel baths and free public foot-soaking pools, which are ideal after a day on a bike.

The riding is Yilan's greatest asset. To the west, the Northern Cross-Island Highway climbs into the mountains toward Daxi, a classic route of bends and views. Along the coast, the old road to Taipei follows the sea cliffs through tunnels and past fishing villages, while the long Hsuehshan Tunnel, almost thirteen kilometres, speeds traffic through the mountains on the expressway, but it is not open to small scooters. South, the coastal cliffs of the Suhua road toward Hualien offer some of the most spectacular sea views in Asia, though landslides and rockfalls make it unpredictable.

Typhoons are the main hazard from July to October, and heavy rain can close mountain roads for days, so check the forecast. Fuel is easy in a city of nearly a hundred thousand people. The best months are spring and autumn, and it is worth planning for at least one wet day.
t.joshua tree village@34.1,-116.3:
Joshua Tree Village is the little desert town at the western gate of Joshua Tree National Park, a place of low buildings, rock shops, cafes, vintage stores and art galleries, where the desert light seems to have drawn a good many musicians, painters and hikers. It sits at about twenty-seven hundred feet in the high Mojave, where the air is dry and clear, the nights are cold, and the horizon is a long line of boulders and yucca. It has a relaxed, slightly eccentric feel.

The tree that gives the place its name is not really a tree but a giant yucca, with spiky green leaves and a twisted, branching trunk. Mormon settlers are said to have named it after the biblical Joshua, seeing the outstretched arms as a gesture of prayer. The trees grow only in the Mojave Desert, and they thrive at this elevation, forming open woodlands that, in spring, burst with creamy white flowers. The surrounding hills are piles of rounded granite boulders, which attract rock climbers from around the world.

Park Boulevard enters the park a short distance from town and runs through the heart of it, across a high plateau of boulders, yuccas and desert scrub, with views of distant ranges. The road is smooth, with long gentle bends and low speed limits, and it passes the Hidden Valley, Jumbo Rocks and the Cholla Cactus Garden, where the spiny plants glow in the low sun. Traffic is heavy in spring and on weekends, and there are cyclists and climbers on the road. Wind can be strong, and dust storms occasionally sweep across the flats.

Fuel is available in Joshua Tree and in the larger town of Yucca Valley, about eleven kilometres away, and it is important to fill up before entering the park, where there are no stations. Cafes and shops line the highway, and the nearby ghost-town-turned-film-set of Pioneertown is a fun detour. Summer temperatures can exceed forty degrees Celsius, so ride in the cool months, from October to May. The night skies are dark and clear, with a dense spread of stars, and the sunrise over the boulders is a good reason to get up early.
t.hidden valley@34.0,-116.2:
Hidden Valley is a small, boulder-ringed basin in Joshua Tree National Park, and it looks, appropriately enough, like a place a person might hide something. Piles of pale monzogranite, rounded by weathering into stacked blocks and domes, form a natural wall around a flat of grass and desert shrubs, with a one-mile loop trail running through it. The local legend says that cattle rustlers used the valley to hide stolen herds in the late nineteenth century, behind rock walls that made a natural corral, and that a rancher named Bill Keys later improved the site for his own cattle. The story is well worn, but the setting makes it easy to believe.

Joshua trees are the star of the park, and here they stand scattered around the boulders, their branches twisted into odd shapes. They are not trees at all, but a kind of yucca, and they only grow in the Mojave Desert. The name is said to have been given by Mormon settlers, who thought the arms reached out like the biblical Joshua. Climbers love this part of the park, and on any weekend morning you will see them bouldering on the rock faces, chalk bags swinging.

Park Boulevard is the road through. It runs north-south through the heart of the park, a smooth, gently rolling ribbon with wide curves, long views and a desert palette of tan and olive. It is not a technical ride, but the combination of boulders, Joshua trees and open sky is remarkable. In spring, if there has been rain, wildflowers cover the ground. Summer is brutally hot, with midday temperatures over forty degrees, so ride early or late, and in winter, mornings can be near freezing.

Twentynine Palms, about seventeen kilometres to the north, is the nearest sizeable town, with fuel, supermarkets and restaurants, and the town of Joshua Tree, on the west side, has more cafes and shops. A park entrance fee is charged, and the car park at Hidden Valley is small, so come early. Carry plenty of water, wear a hat, and leave the cacti alone. The silence here is one of the best things about the place.
t.keys view@33.9,-116.2:
Keys View sits on the crest of the Little San Bernardino Mountains at about 1,580 metres, and the view from it is the longest in Joshua Tree National Park. Below you the land falls away sharply into the Coachella Valley, a broad, flat basin of date palms, golf courses and spreading towns, with Palm Springs on the near side and the Salton Sea glinting far off to the south on a clear day. Beyond lie the high peaks of the San Jacinto and San Gorgonio mountains, snow-capped for much of the winter.

The drop beneath your feet is not an accident. The long, straight line at the foot of the mountains is the San Andreas Fault, the great crack in the earth where the Pacific and North American plates grind slowly past each other. You can see the line of the fault from the viewpoint, a dark stripe of vegetation where the water collects. The valley is a rift, and the mountains are on the move, though at the pace of a fingernail growing. The viewpoint takes its name from Bill Keys, a homesteader who ran a ranch, a mill and a family in the park for decades.

The road to Keys View is a spur off Park Boulevard, climbing about five miles from Park Boulevard in easy bends through juniper and yucca. It is a quiet, well-surfaced road, with short climbs and a clear view ahead, and a good ride on any bike. Haze can obscure the view, particularly in summer, because smog from the Los Angeles basin drifts in from the west. The best time is after a storm, in winter or early spring, when the air is crisp and the mountains stand out sharp. The wind at the top can be fierce, and the temperature several degrees cooler than at the desert floor.

There are no services at Keys View, only a car park, toilets and a short paved path to the viewpoint. Carry water and warm layers, because it can be breezy even on a hot day. Sunset is the favourite hour, when the valley lights come on.
t.cholla cactus garden@33.9,-115.9:
The Cholla Cactus Garden is the sort of place that makes you slow down on instinct. Over a flat expanse of the Pinto Basin, thousands of teddy bear cholla stand in dense, silvery stands, each one a spiny cluster of jointed stems that glows with a golden halo when the light hits it from behind. They look soft, which is the trap. The spines are barbed, the joints detach at a touch, and anyone who has met one will tell you it does not feel cuddly. A short loop trail winds through the thickest part, and you should stay on it.

The garden belongs to the Colorado Desert, the lower and hotter part of the park, where the vegetation is more sparse and the colours more muted than the Joshua trees farther up. Ocotillo, creosote bush and smoke trees dot the washes, and after a wet winter the whole area bursts into bloom in March and April. The best time to visit is in the late afternoon, when the low sun lights the spines and the heat has eased. Sunrise is also magnificent, and quiet.

The ride in is part of the pleasure. Park Boulevard descends from the high Mojave plateau through a long, easy sweep of curves, and as you drop in altitude the air warms and the landscape changes. The road is smooth, with long straights and good visibility, and the traffic is light on weekdays. This is a place where the sky is enormous, and in summer it is also fierce, with midday heat close to fifty degrees on the tarmac, so riding in the early morning or evening is much more comfortable. Watch for wildlife, particularly at dusk, and for loose sand blown across the road.

There is no water or fuel at the garden, only a small car park and a trail. The nearest towns are Twentynine Palms, about twenty-six kilometres away, which has petrol, shops and cafes, and Indio, to the south, which is bigger. Fill up before entering the park, because distances are long and signal is patchy. Bring water, wear a hat, and keep children and pets well away from the plants. If you do get a spine in you, a comb or pair of pliers is the way to remove it.
t.cottonwood spring@33.7,-115.8:
Cottonwood Spring is an oasis in the lower corner of Joshua Tree National Park, where the high Mojave desert gives way to the hotter Colorado Desert, and a small cluster of fan palms and cottonwood trees grows around a spring that has been used for centuries. The Cahuilla people gathered here, grinding seeds and mesquite beans in rock mortars, and the holes can still be seen in the boulders. Later, gold miners camped by the water, and ruins of their mills survive in the hills.

The spring itself is a modest affair, but in a landscape this dry, a patch of shade and a trickle of water are very valuable. Birds come in, from migrating warblers to roadrunners, and bighorn sheep sometimes drink in the early morning. The surroundings are low, open desert of creosote bush, ocotillo and cholla, and in good years in spring, wildflowers cover the ground in yellow, purple and white. A short trail leads to Mastodon Peak, a rocky hill with views over the valley and the old mine workings.

The ride south from the main part of the park is a long, gentle descent, from the stands of Joshua trees through a sloping desert of boulders and into a wide, sandy basin, with the Pinto Basin on one side and the Eagle Mountains rising on the other. The road is smooth, quiet and flowing, with long straights, and it takes you from one ecosystem to another, with the temperature climbing as you drop. At the end, you reach the interstate, and the sudden rush of traffic feels harsh after the silence.

Mecca, to the south, has more services. Summer heat is severe, so ride early, wear light gear and carry plenty of water. The best months are from late October to April, and the night sky is magnificent.
t.santa monica pier@34.0,-118.5:
The longest road in American mythology runs out of land here. Route 66 was commissioned in 1926 to link Chicago with Los Angeles, and as it went through eight states on its two-thousand-mile journey it picked up the nickname the Mother Road. The official end of the highway is a matter of fine print, with the route having been rerouted several times, but the pier at Santa Monica carries a sign calling it the End of the Trail, and that is where riders photograph their bikes, so that is where this ride finishes.

The pier itself opened in 1909 and has been a seaside amusement ever since, with a carousel from the 1920s, an amusement park with a solar-powered Ferris wheel, arcades, fishing from the rails, and the sound of gulls and the hiss of surf beneath the boards. It has been repaired and rebuilt after storms and fires. The Pacific stretches out to the horizon, and on a clear evening the sun sets in a long orange ribbon over the water, while the mountains of Malibu line the coast to the north.

Route 66 was decommissioned in 1985, replaced by the interstates, but Americans refused to let it go, and the old road, in pieces, has become a pilgrimage. Reaching this point after a long trip across the desert is a reward in itself. The last miles through Los Angeles are slow and urban, with traffic lights, lane splitting by locals, and a lot of cars, so choose your hours carefully. Rush hours can be dense, and the best time to arrive is in the late morning or the evening.

Everything you need is here, including fuel, though prices in California are among the highest in the country. Parking for motorcycles near the pier is easier than for cars, but there are fees and rules, so look at the signs. The Venice boardwalk, with its muscle gym, skate park and street performers, is a short ride south. Fresh seafood and tacos are easy to find, and in summer, the marine layer can bring cool grey mornings, so a light jacket is welcome. The beach is wide, and the Pacific is cold, even in August.
t.cova de la catxupa abric i@38.8,0.1:
The Marina Alta is the northern Costa Blanca at its most mixed: villas on every slope, a ribbon of coast running from Moraira to Jávea, and just behind it, farm terraces, dry stone walls and small rock shelters where prehistoric people left their mark. The Cova de la Catxupa, near Teulada and Benitachell, is one of them, a shelter in the hills a few kilometres from the sea, listed with the other Mediterranean rock art of the Iberian Peninsula.

Teulada is the inland twin of the resort of Moraira, an old village of white houses with a fortified church at its heart. Across the hills, Gata de Gorgos is known for two crafts: guitar making, with several workshops building Spanish guitars, and weaving of palm and cane into baskets, hats and furniture, sold in shops along the main road. Benitachell sits below the headland of the Cumbre del Sol, with cliffs dropping straight into the sea.

The Marina Alta was once raisin country. Moscatel grapes were dried in the sun and under riuraus, long arched porches attached to farmhouses, and many of them survive. The wine and the mistela, a sweet fortified drink, are still made, and the farmhouses are a lovely sight in the landscape. The light here is bright, the sea glitters in the distance, and in late winter the almond blossom paints the valleys pink and white.

Riding here is mixed. The coastal roads are busy, particularly in summer, and urbanisations mean frequent junctions, roundabouts and slow traffic. But head a few kilometres inland and the roads become quieter, climbing into the hills with good bends and views back to the coast. The roads toward Jalón and the Vall de Pop, and the climbs into the mountains behind, are well loved by local riders.

Teulada is a town of nearly fifteen thousand with fuel and services, and Gata de Gorgos has everything you need too. Moraira and Jávea offer seafood restaurants, beaches and cafés, and the area is lively all year round thanks to the many foreign residents.
t.c5 area between the ravines of torrevell:
Menorca is a gentler island than its neighbours, and the Talaiotic culture left behind a remarkable landscape of stone monuments that UNESCO recognised in 2023. These are the talaiots, round or square towers of dry stone, the taulas, great T-shaped stone altars, and the navetas, boat-shaped tombs, all dating from the second and first millennia BC. Nobody knows exactly what the people who built them believed, but the sheer number is astonishing for an island that you can cross by car in an hour. C5 is one of the numbered zones of that heritage landscape, in the area between the ravines of Torrevella, south of Alaior.

The land here is low, open and windswept, a patchwork of small fields divided by dry stone walls, and the walls themselves are an old craft, still repaired by hand. Holm oaks and wild olives stand in clumps, and the soil is red and stony. The famous north wind, the tramontana, can blow for days and bend the trees into permanent leaning shapes. The smell in summer is of hot stone and thyme, and in the evening the light on the walls is gold. Menorca is a UNESCO biosphere reserve, and its quieter roads and bridleways make it a place for slow travel.

The riding is simple and pleasant. The island's main road runs along the spine from Maó to Ciutadella, and smaller roads branch off to farms and coves with a mix of gentle curves and straights, tight stone walls on either side. Speeds are low and traffic can be thick in July and August, with hire cars and cyclists. The surface is generally good, though minor roads can be narrow and rough, and tourist coaches need patience.

Alaior, about five kilometres away, is a sizeable town of eight and a half thousand with fuel, supermarkets and a good market. It is also known for its cheese, a mild, slightly salty cow's milk cheese that has its own protected name, and for its ice cream. Spring is the best season, with wildflowers and warm days, and September is calm and warm after the crowds have left. Winter can be wet and windy, and some places close.
Menorca is the quiet island of the Balearics, and its south coast is cut by ravines, the barrancs, that run down from the limestone plateau to the sea in narrow, green clefts. The central-south area is where they are most impressive: Algendar, Trebalúger, Binigaus and others, each a steep-sided channel with wild olive, holm oak and a trickle of water in the bottom, ending in a small beach. The whole island was declared a Biosphere Reserve in 1993, and the old walking path that circles it, the Camí de Cavalls, passes by the mouths of most of them.

Getting here by motorcycle is simple but slow. The island has one main road running along its spine from Maó to Ciutadella, and from it small lanes drop toward the coast between dry stone walls, in a pattern that has hardly changed for centuries. Those lanes are narrow, often with blind corners and the occasional tractor, and speed limits are low and enforced. The north wind, the Tramuntana, can blow hard in winter and spring, so check the forecast before you set out. Summer brings crowds and heat, while May, June and late September are the sweet spots for a quiet ride.

Alaior, seven kilometres off, has nearly nine thousand people and is where you buy fuel and food. It is the home of the island's cheese, a soft, tangy variety with a protected name that comes in square blocks. Ferreries, with over four thousand, is another handy town. The island also holds an extraordinary Bronze Age legacy in its stone talayots and taulas, towers and T-shaped monuments built over three thousand years ago, now recognised by UNESCO, and many of them stand beside the very roads you ride.

Try the local gin, flavoured with juniper and made on the island since the British period in the eighteenth century, when the Royal Navy was stationed at Maó. Menorcans also claim, with some conviction, that mayonnaise was born in Maó. Whether or not that is true, a plate of grilled fish with a dollop of it on a terrace above a barranc is a very good way to end a day.
t.cova de la catxupa abric ii@38.8,0.1:
Teulada is the town, and Moraira is its seaside annexe, and between them they hold most of what people know about this slice of the Costa Blanca. The Catxupa shelter lies just outside the town, which has some fourteen and a half thousand residents, many of them northern Europeans who came for the sun and stayed. The old centre of Teulada, though, remains a Valencian one, with a fortified parish church and narrow lanes that fill with the smell of coffee and baking at midday.

The second shelter in the Catxupa group is a small overhang under the limestone slopes that fall toward the sea. The Levantine tradition of painting in red on rock shelters is found all along this coast, and this is one of the closer ones to the sea. It is a reminder that before holidaymakers, before the Romans and Moors, these slopes were hunting country, with the coast visible from the hills and game running through the scrub.

Moraira, a short ride down the hill, is the charming part. It is a former fishing village with a little castle on the point, built in the eighteenth century to guard against raiders from the sea, and a beach protected by a rocky headland. The nearby cape of Cap d'Or is a dramatic spit of land that looks like a dragon's back, and the cliffs near the Cap de la Nau, to the north, are among the finest on this coast. Moscatel grapes grow on the terraces, and the sweet wine made from them is worth a bottle.

The riding is a mix of gentle coastal bends and quick climbs inland. Roads here are good and mostly well maintained, though the traffic can be heavy in July and August, when everyone is trying to reach the beach. If you want peace, come in spring or autumn, or go inland by the back roads toward Benissa and Xàbia, which are quieter and more scenic.

Teulada has pumps, supermarkets, cafés and restaurants, so fuel and lunch are no trouble. Bring water for the walk to the shelter.
t.cova de la catxupa abric iii@38.8,0.1:
Behind Teulada the land rises sharply, and the third shelter in the Catxupa series sits where the first foothills begin. It is not an obvious place for an ancient painted site. The coast is only a few kilometres away, and the view toward the sea is partly built over. But the Levantine rock art tradition ran right down to this edge of the Mediterranean, and the overhangs of the hills here were used by people long before anyone built a villa.

Think of it as a gateway. A few minutes inland from Teulada the road starts climbing, and within half an hour you are in a landscape of terraces, almond trees and narrow lanes more typical of the Marina Alta interior. The Coll de Rates is the great local climb, a pass of around six hundred metres on the road between Parcent and Tàrbena, and it is a favourite with cyclists and motorcyclists alike. From the top the view back toward the Mediterranean is worth the hairpins, and a bar there serves a decent coffee and a plate of olives.

The area is also known for its wine. Moscatel de Alejandría, the sweet muscat grape, thrives on these slopes, and the villages of the Jalón valley make a wine that tastes of raisins and orange peel. Raisins are still dried in sheds called riurau, open-fronted porches that you will spot on farms beside the road, a tradition that dates back to the Moors.

Roads on this side of the hills are twisty and sometimes narrow, with surfaces that vary. Traffic is light on weekdays, but on Sundays you will share the bends with cyclists, so keep your speed sensible. In summer the middle of the day can be punishing, and in winter the mountains can be cold and damp. Autumn is the best season, with warm days and clear air.

Teulada is only three kilometres away and has everything you need: fuel, cafés, supermarkets. Carry water, as the shelters have none.
t.imperial tombs of the ming and qing dyna:
Long before the Manchus took Beijing, they had a home, and it was in the green, hilly country east of Shenyang, where the Hun river comes out of the Changbai foothills. Yongling, the Qing dynasty's earliest imperial tomb, stands there in the county of Xinbin, built at the start of the seventeenth century and expanded afterwards to house the ancestors of Nurhaci, the chief who united the Jurchen tribes and founded the line that would rule China until 1912. It is an old-fashioned ceremonial complex, with walls, a stone bridge, spirit-way sculptures and a tomb mound behind, set against a wooded hillside, and it makes a clear point: before they were emperors of China, these people were mountain chieftains.

The tomb belongs, with the Ming tombs near Beijing and other Qing tombs in Shenyang and Hebei, to the World Heritage group of the imperial tombs of the Ming and Qing dynasties. The ride also takes in Wunu Mountain City, a mountain fortress built by the earlier kingdom of Goguryeo, a thousand years before the Manchu era, high on a flat-topped cliff near Huanren. Together the two give a picture of how this north-eastern borderland has always been a place where powers met.

I should be honest about the riding. Taking a foreign motorcycle across China requires permits, a guide and temporary licences, and few visitors manage it independently, so most riders here will use a local rental or a tour. The reward, for those who do, is a countryside of forested hills, maize and rice fields, small Manchu villages and winding river roads, with the whole area beautifully red and gold in October. Summers are green and humid, and winters are bitterly cold, with snow and ice, so the best months are May, June and September.

Fushun, the nearest big city, is an old coal and industrial town, and Xinbin has a few fuel stations and restaurants of its own, but facilities thin out in the hills, so fill the tank when you can. Northeastern Chinese cooking is hearty: pork stewed with pickled cabbage, dumplings with thick wrappers, and river fish from the mountain streams, washed down with a local beer. In the villages, drying corn hangs in golden strings from the eaves, a bright detail on a grey autumn day.
t.malibu@34.0,-118.8:
Twenty-one miles of the Pacific Coast Highway pass through Malibu, and most of them are within sight of the sea. The road squeezes between the steep brown slopes of the Santa Monica Mountains and a narrow ribbon of sand, a mix of beach houses, small plazas, surf breaks and sudden gaps with a view over the water. The town itself has about thirteen thousand people, a city of film stars and surfers, and a strong feeling of being at the edge of something. It was once a ranch owned by the Rindge family, who held off development for decades, and the land was divided only in the 1920s, after the state forced a public road through it.

The highway is famous, and for good reason, but it is not a race track. At weekends the road fills with sightseers, delivery vans, cyclists and drivers looking for a place to park, and there are speed limits, traffic lights and patrols, with fines that are not small. The coast road has had a bad record for crashes. A good plan is to go early on a weekday, when the light comes slanting over the hills and the sea is pale blue, and the road is almost clear. In late spring and early summer the morning fog, called June gloom, can sit over the shore until noon.

For something with more bends, take one of the canyon roads that climb into the mountains. Malibu Canyon Road, Decker, Latigo and Mulholland Highway all twist up through chaparral and oak, with drops, cambers and tight corners that reward a rider with some care, and with the sea sparkling far below as you climb. They are narrow, and the surface can be rough, with gravel and fallen rock, and in places there are no barriers. Fires have swept through the mountains repeatedly, including the Woolsey fire of 2018 and the Palisades fire of 2025, leaving scars on the hills and homes, so you will see burned areas and rebuilding. Check the road status in fire season and after heavy rain, when landslides can close sections.

Fuel in Malibu is among the most expensive in California, so fill up in Santa Monica or Oxnard if you can, though there are stations along the highway. For a break, a beach cafe or a fish shack near the pier serves tacos and clam chowder with a view. The Getty Villa, a museum of ancient art in a replica Roman villa, lies a few miles south and is free to enter, with booking.
t.natural site@38.8,1.4:
This is the end of the island where the beach clubs thin out and the landscape opens up into flat white salt flats, a lagoon full of flamingos in winter and spring, and a long beach called Es Cavallet where the dunes hold their shape.

The salt is the clue to the island's history. Phoenician settlers arrived about the eighth century BC and founded a trading settlement, and the pans have been worked ever since, with Carthaginians, Romans, Moors and Catalans all taking their share. The salt was one of Ibiza's reasons for existing, and it is why the town, Dalt Vila, its fortified old quarter, and the Puig des Molins necropolis, a great Phoenician and Punic cemetery on the edge of the city, are now part of a UNESCO site that also includes the sea-grass meadows around the island. The Posidonia, a flowering plant that grows in vast underwater fields, keeps the water here clear and turquoise.

For riding, Ibiza is better than its reputation. The roads are small, tarred and fairly empty outside high season. The route south from Ibiza town towards Sant Josep passes through pine, fig and carob groves, with red earth and low stone walls, and the road along the salt pans is flat, open and breezy. In July and August traffic is heavy and the car parks fill, so aim for May, June or late September, when the water is warm and the light is gentle.

Ibiza town, thirteen kilometres away, has everything in the way of fuel, food and rooms, and Sant Josep, a little closer, has a few pumps. The island has no great mountains, though Sa Talaia reaches about 475 metres, and you can see Formentera across the strait on a clear day.
t.ventura@34.3,-119.2:
Mission San Buenaventura, founded in 1782 by Father Junípero Serra, was the last of the missions he established, and its church and garden are a quiet, peaceful corner in the middle of the town. Ventura Pier, built in 1872, is the longest wooden pier in California, a long wooden promenade that pokes out into the Pacific, and fishermen and walkers stroll along it.

The sea here is rich and the weather is mild. The Channel Islands, a group of rugged islands that form a national park, lie about thirty kilometres offshore, and boats leave from Ventura Harbor to carry visitors to them. On the way you may see dolphins, whales and seabirds. To the north, the road follows the coast through Rincon, a famous surf break, with the ocean on one side and the cliffs on the other, and the highway runs under the shadow of the Santa Ynez mountains. Inland, Highway 33 leads up the Ventura river valley to Ojai, a little town with orange groves and an arts scene.

The riding is of two kinds. The coastal run on Highway 101 is fast, wide and busy, with beautiful views of the sea and the islands, and it is a fine way to get north to Santa Barbara, but the traffic can be dense, especially at weekends. The inland roads, particularly Highway 33 and the smaller roads in the hills, are tighter, with curves, climbs and wide vistas of orange and avocado groves. The surface is generally good, though sections are rough, and in autumn the Santa Ana winds can be strong and hot.

Fuel, food and coffee are easy, with Ventura offering every service, and the old downtown has a good selection of cafés, restaurants and breweries. Fish tacos and fresh seafood are staples, and a coffee on the pier in the morning is a good start. Try an avocado, as the area is a big producer.

Walk to the end of the pier at sunset. The sky turns orange, the islands become shadows, and the sea is calm. It is the very picture of the California coast.
t.barstow@34.9,-117.0:
Barstow is a railroad town that happens to have a highway running through it, and you can feel the trains in the place: freight cars rumble past day and night, and the yards on the edge of town are among the largest in California. The settlement grew up in the 1880s as a junction on the Santa Fe line, and the Casa del Desierto, a Harvey House hotel and station built in the early twentieth century in the Spanish Mission style, still stands beside the tracks and houses a Route 66 museum. It gives a good idea of what travel in the age of steam looked like, with fine dining and uniformed waitresses for passengers changing trains in the desert.

The Mojave surrounds the town, a plain of creosote bush and rock with low brown ranges on the horizon. It is hot and dry in summer, with temperatures regularly above forty degrees, and cold and windy in winter, with occasional snow on the mountains. Spring after good rains can bring a carpet of wildflowers. For a rider on Route 66 it is a place where the road empties out, long straight miles of broken, patched asphalt running parallel to the railway and the interstate, with abandoned filling stations and shuttered motels.

Barstow is a practical stop. It has plenty of fuel, restaurants, motels and shops, mostly strung along the old route and the interstate, and with a population of more than twenty thousand it is the largest town for a long way in either direction. Many riders stay overnight before or after the long desert crossing. The Mother Road Museum has old photographs, signs and relics of the highway's glory days, and is worth an hour.

Nearby, the old silver mining town of Calico, now a tourist attraction, stands on a hillside north-east of town, with its wooden buildings and gift shops, and the Bagdad Cafe, made famous by a film, is farther east along the old road at Newberry Springs. West of Barstow, the route climbs toward Victorville and the Cajon Pass.

Wind is a constant companion in the high desert, and it can be fierce in the afternoons, so keep a firm grip on the bars and expect to be buffeted by passing trucks. Water bottles and sunscreen are as important as a spare tyre.
t.san bernardino@34.1,-117.3:
Hamburgers changed the world here, or at least the way Americans eat. The first McDonald's restaurant opened in San Bernardino in 1940, a drive-in run by two brothers, and the idea of fast, standardised, cheap food that began on this corner went on to spread around the globe. The original site is gone, but a small museum on Route 66 tells the story, and it is a curious pilgrimage for any rider following the old highway. The city itself is large, a place of more than two hundred thousand people stretched across a plain at the foot of the San Bernardino Mountains.

The mountains are the real attraction. They rise abruptly to more than three thousand metres, and in winter their peaks are dusted with snow while palm trees wave in the valley below. The Cajon Pass, the gap through which Route 66 and the railway arrive from the desert, is just to the north, and the road drops from the high Mojave to the Los Angeles basin in a few miles. The long descent by old Route 66 is a pleasure, with gentle bends and wide views, though traffic on the interstate beside it can be heavy.

The Santa Ana winds are the local peril. Hot, dry gusts blowing down from the desert in autumn can make riding unpleasant and fire risk severe, and the hills around the city have burned many times. On a clear day after a storm the air is crystalline, and you can see the snow on Mount Baldy and the long line of the foothills. Smog can be thick in summer, particularly in the afternoon.

San Bernardino is a major road junction with fuel stations on every corner, and you can find food, mechanics and motels without difficulty. The old Route 66 follows Foothill Boulevard through a long chain of towns toward Pasadena and Santa Monica, with palm-lined avenues, mid-century motels and neon signs, many of them restored. Traffic is dense, and lane splitting is legal in California under certain conditions, though riders should take care in the stop-and-go flow.

The Mojave section behind you was the hard part, a long, lonely run of heat and wind, and the city's lights are a relief. A cold drink and a plate of tacos from a roadside stand are the proper reward.
t.los angeles southern california@34.7,-11:
Joshua trees and creosote bush spread out toward a horizon cut by the San Bernardino Mountains to the south, and on a clear morning the snow on the higher ridges looks borrowed from another state. Adelanto, a town of some thirty-odd thousand, is the sensible place to sort fuel and a breakfast burrito; Victorville sits right next to it with more of everything.

This is where the Big Bear loops begin their long haul upward. Riders coming from the Los Angeles side usually cross the mountains through Cajon Pass, drop into the desert, and then turn back up toward the rim, so the flat ground here is a kind of warm-up lap, a lull before the road starts to climb through pines. The Mojave River, which spends most of its life underground, makes a long arc nearby, and old Route 66 once strung together the little desert towns along it. If you have an appetite for a detour, the National Trails Highway still carries traces of that road.

Be honest about the weather. Summer afternoons out here are hot enough that the bike wants to sit in the shade, and spring brings wind that leans on you from the west with real conviction. Early morning is the right hour to leave: the air is cold and clean, the light is low and long, and you reach the mountains before the heat does. In winter, check the pass conditions before you climb, because the rim roads above can ice over while the desert floor sits in sunshine.

The finish of a day here tends to be quiet. You come back down to a plain full of warehouses and solar fields, with the last light turning the mountains pink, and the feeling is of having been somewhere genuinely high. Water is easy to buy in town, and it is worth carrying more than you think you need, because the gap between gas stations can feel longer on a hot road than it looks on a map.
t.kootenay national park@51.0,-116.0:
There is a place on this road where the colour of the ground changes from grey to rust. Kootenay National Park, on the western side of the Continental Divide, is the quieter neighbour of Banff, and Highway 93 South threads through it for about ninety kilometres from the Vermilion Pass to the hot springs at Radium. The stretch around Marble Canyon is the heart of it, with a deep, narrow limestone gorge and, close by, the Paint Pots, where iron-rich springs stain the earth ochre, and where the First Nations once gathered pigment to trade.

The riding is excellent. The highway rises and falls through forest and past avalanche slopes, mostly smooth and well-banked, with plenty of long sweepers and good sight lines. In 1968, a big fire burned the Vermilion Pass area, and walking the little interpretive trail there shows the way the forest regrows, with silvery dead snags standing among the young pines. Traffic is moderate, and the speed limit is low because wildlife is common: bighorn sheep, mountain goats, black bears, and sometimes elk or moose beside the road.

Fuel is a real consideration. There are no pumps inside the park for long stretches, so fill the tank before you enter, either in Banff or Radium Hot Springs. The park gate requires a national parks pass, which you buy at the booth or beforehand, and you should keep it displayed. Snow can fall on the pass any month of the year, and the road is open all year but often requires winter tyres from late autumn to spring.

Best times are late June to September. In June, the waterfalls are loud with melt; in September, the larches on the high slopes turn gold, a fine sight if the light is right. Dress in layers, since the mountains can be cool in the morning and warm by noon.
t.radium hot springs@50.6,-116.1:
You smell Radium Hot Springs before you see it, or so it seems: faint sulphur, wood smoke, hot tarmac. The village sits where the Kootenay valley opens to the broad Columbia, and the road from the north drops through Sinclair Canyon, a dramatic notch in red rock, so narrow that the highway squeezes through with barely a shoulder. It is the best entrance to any town on the loop.

The springs themselves are the reason it exists. The hot pool, fed from a spring that comes out at around forty degrees, has been used for centuries by the Ktunaxa people, and in the early twentieth century it became a spa. Today the big pool, built into the canyon wall, is a lovely thing at the end of a day in the saddle: warm water, cool air, cliffs above. In the village, bighorn sheep wander the streets and lawns, so watch for them at dusk and in the morning, and drive gently.

The village is small, and the nearest bigger town is Invermere, about twelve kilometres north on the shore of Lake Windermere, where you will find more shops and services. Radium itself has motels, cafes and fuel stations, plus a couple of good places for a hearty meal, and it is a lively stop in summer, busy with families and riders.

East of here the road climbs back into the mountains and into the park, while to the south the Columbia valley is a broad corridor of grass and wetlands, an important bird area, with the Rockies on one side and the Purcells on the other. Heat can be sharp in July and August, and storms build in the afternoon, so aim to arrive in the early evening. Come in the golden hour and the canyon walls glow like embers.
t.columbia icefield@52.2,-117.2:
A raindrop that lands on the Columbia Icefield has three possible destinations, and it is hard to find a better place to say so. From the snowy dome at the heart of this ice, meltwater drains to the Pacific by the Columbia, to the Arctic by the Athabasca and Mackenzie, and to Hudson Bay via the Saskatchewan. The icefield itself sits astride the Continental Divide, a plateau of ice some hundreds of metres deep, feeding half a dozen big glaciers, of which the Athabasca is the one you can see from the highway.

The Icefields Parkway, Highway 93, is the road that takes you there, and it is rightly counted among the great motorcycle roads of the world. It runs between Lake Louise and Jasper for about 230 kilometres, through a procession of peaks, glacier-fed lakes, turquoise rivers and waterfalls. The surface is smooth, the bends long and open, and the speed limit low, which is fine: you will not want to hurry. Wildlife is part of the show, with bighorn sheep, black bears, mountain goats and elk beside the road. Sunwapta Pass, at about 2,030 metres, marks the boundary between Banff and Jasper national parks, a short ride north of the icefield.

The Athabasca Glacier has retreated more than a kilometre in the last century, and markers beside the path show where the ice reached in different years. The glacier is an easy walk from the car park, but crevasses and fast-moving meltwater make it dangerous to go far without a guide, so heed the signs. The visitor centre across the road has a cafe and information, and there is a glass walkway at a lookout nearby, though riders may prefer to spend the money on a good lunch.

The nearest pumps are at Saskatchewan River Crossing to the south, which is seasonal, and at Jasper, a long way to the north, so fill the tank at Lake Louise or Jasper and top up when you can. The parkway is open all year, but snow can fall in any month, and winter tyres are required in winter. Dress warmly: the wind off the ice is cold even on a sunny July day.
t.soller@39.8,2.7:
Sóller lies in a basin of orange and lemon trees, enclosed by the highest peaks of the Serra de Tramuntana, and it is the nearest thing in Mallorca to a green bowl. For centuries the only way in or out was a mountain pass or a boat, and the isolation made the valley rich and strange. Local merchants sold oranges to France and returned with money and ideas, and some of the town's buildings show it, including a modernista church front and a bank in a style borrowed from Barcelona. The old wooden train from Palma, which opened in 1912, still runs through tunnels and viaducts to the station in the middle of town, and a small tram carries passengers down to the harbour at Port de Sóller.

For motorcyclists, the road to Sóller is one of the great pleasures of the island. The old road over the pass, the Coll de Sóller, climbs in a long series of hairpins through olives and pines, with views down to the sea, and it is a lovely, demanding ride. Since the late 1990s, a toll tunnel has offered a quicker route under the mountain, and traffic has thinned on the old road accordingly. From Sóller, the Ma-10 runs north-east along the spine of the range, through Fornalutx, a village of stone and green shutters that is often called one of the prettiest in Spain, and on towards Lluc and the northern coast.

The Tramuntana was made a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2011 as a cultural landscape, because of the centuries of terracing and water management that shaped the slopes. You can see the stone terraces from the road, rising in steps above the town. Spring is the most beautiful time, with almond blossom early and wild flowers later, though cyclists crowd the roads then, so ride with care. Summer brings heavy tourist traffic, particularly on the coast road, and the best hours are early morning and evening.

With almost fourteen thousand people, Sóller has fuel and every kind of food. Order the freshly squeezed orange juice, which is made from the local fruit, and a sweet ensaïmada, the spiral pastry that is the island's emblem. A leisurely coffee on the square, beneath the church, is a good place to rest between passes.
t.johnston canyon@51.2,-115.8:
Johnston Canyon is a slot in the limestone of Banff National Park, and the whole attraction is that a path has been built into it. Steel catwalks bolted to the canyon wall lead you over the creek, with turquoise water rushing below and the rock close enough to touch. After about a kilometre you reach the Lower Falls, a small drop into a pool, and after a longer walk, the Upper Falls, a taller plunge of about thirty metres. Further on, the Ink Pots are a cluster of cold green springs in a meadow, a pleasing finish if you have the legs.

The creek has cut its gorge through the Rocky Mountain limestone over thousands of years, using the force of meltwater and the grinding of stones. The rock is pale grey, streaked with orange and black, and in places the walls close over your head. Spray cools the air, moss grows in the cracks and in winter the waterfalls freeze into tall blue columns, which draw ice climbers and people with cleated boots. Dippers, small grey birds that walk underwater, are sometimes seen hunting insects in the creek.

The canyon is on the Bow Valley Parkway, which runs along the north side of the Bow River between Banff and Lake Louise. It is a quieter, slower alternative to the Trans-Canada Highway, with a speed limit of sixty kilometres an hour and long stretches of forest broken by views of the Bow and the ridge of Castle Mountain. For a rider, it is an easy, relaxed ride, ideal for early morning when wildlife, from elk to black bears, grazes beside the road. There are seasonal restrictions to protect wildlife, which can close sections of the parkway to vehicles at certain times, so check Parks Canada's current notices before you go. A park pass is needed for any stop in the national park.

Johnston Canyon is one of the busiest sites in the park, and the car park fills quickly in summer. Arrive before nine in the morning or after five in the evening to avoid the worst of the crowds, and keep an eye on the bike when you park. Do not approach any animals, particularly bears and elk, and carry bear spray if you intend to walk.

Services are limited. Banff, about twenty kilometres away, is the nearest large town, and Lake Louise has a station further west. Fill the tank in Banff before you set out, and enjoy the cool air under the pines.
t.castle junction@51.3,-115.9:
Castle Junction is a crossroads in the forest at the foot of Castle Mountain, and the mountain is the reason you remember it. The peak rises as a long, battlemented wall of layered limestone, about 2,700 metres at its highest, with ledges and towers that really do suggest a fortress. It was named in the 1850s by a geologist who saw the shape from the valley, and in 1946 Canada renamed it Mount Eisenhower to honour the general, an unpopular change that was partly reversed in 1979 when the name was restored to the main mountain, with the Eisenhower name left for one tower.

The junction is where the Bow Valley Parkway meets Highway 93, the road that runs south through the Kootenay National Park toward Radium Hot Springs and the Columbia Valley. It is a quiet place, with a few buildings, a little roadside accommodation and the ghost of a larger story. During the First World War, a camp near here held Ukrainian and other European immigrants who had been declared enemy aliens, and who were made to work building roads and clearing land. A small marker remembers the internment, and it is a sober thing to read in a place of such beauty.

For motorcyclists, this is a good point at which to decide between two excellent rides. Go west along the parkway toward Lake Louise and the road is an easy, flowing route through the forest. Turn south on Highway 93 and you climb to Vermilion Pass, cross the Continental Divide into Kootenay National Park, and descend into a landscape of burnt forest, bright flowers, and a red-stained canyon. t.banyalbufar@39.7,2.5:

t.deia@39.7,2.6:
Robert Graves, the English poet and author of I, Claudius, lived in Deià for much of his life, and he is buried in the little cemetery on the hill beside the church. t.es colomer@39.9,3.1:

t.formentor beach@39.9,3.1:

t.taroko gorge@24.2,121.5:

t.hehuanshan wuling@24.1,121.3:

t.nanfangao@24.6,121.9:
Nanfang'ao is a fishing harbour tucked into a bay on the north-east coast of Taiwan, and it is still more working port than tourist attraction. t.qingshui cliffs@24.2,121.7:
The Qingshui Cliffs are where Taiwan's eastern mountains simply stop and the Pacific begins. The rock face rises almost a kilometre straight out of the sea, a wall of grey and white marble and gneiss streaked with vegetation, and the road runs along its flank, cut into the cliff, with a drop of hundreds of metres on one side. t.ruisui@23.5,121.4:

t.chishang@23.1,121.2:

t.palomar east grade@33.3,-116.9:

t.lake henshaw view@33.2,-116.8:

Later it became ranchland, and the old stage route from the east to San Diego passed through, a hard road for settlers arriving across the desert. Today cattle still graze on the grass, and the roads are quiet.

For a rider, the view from the road is an invitation to slow down. State Route 76 here is a well-surfaced highway with long curves, gentle gradients and open vistas, and it is a pleasure in the cool of the morning or the warmth of the evening. Pull off at a safe spot, take off your helmet and listen. The valley is wide and quiet, and for a moment the whole region seems to be holding its breath.
t.julian pie and food@33.1,-116.6:

t.dana point@33.5,-117.7:
Dana Point has a better claim to literary fame than most harbour towns in Orange County. He described the bluff here as the only romantic spot on the coast, and the town took his name. The corners are gentle, speeds are low and traffic can be heavy, particularly on summer weekends, so patience is the main skill. Start early, ride north with the ocean on your left and take your time.
t.shitiping@23.5,121.5:
Shitiping means roughly stone steps terrace, and that already tells you a lot about the place. It sits on Taiwan's east coast, where the Coastal Mountain Range drops almost straight into the Pacific, and the highway squeezes itself between rock and sea. The area belongs to the long, wild stretch of Provincial Highway 11, the road that runs south from Hualien towards Taitung with the ocean on one side nearly all the way.

The surface is generally good, the bends are open and flowing, and the sea view is constant: a deep Pacific blue in the morning, turning silver-grey under cloud. There are tunnels and cuttings, a few tight spots at the headlands and a lot of rolling coastal tarmac where you can settle into a rhythm. Traffic is mostly local trucks, scooters and cyclists, the last of whom come here for exactly the same reason you do. t.mausoleum kbor er roumia@36.6,2.6:
On a low hill west of Algiers, above the farmland of the Mitidja plain and within sight of the sea, stands a great round tomb of pale stone that the French called the Tombeau de la Chrétienne and the Algerians call Kbor er Roumia, the tomb of the Christian woman. The name is a folk memory rather than a fact, since the monument was built in the first century BC for the Berber king Juba II of Mauretania and his wife Cleopatra Selene, the daughter of Mark Antony and Cleopatra of Egypt. A royal couple with that parentage, ruling a Roman client kingdom from the coast of Africa, is a story that sounds invented but is simply true.

The tomb is a drum about sixty metres across, topped by a stepped cone, and it once stood much higher than it does today. Its walls are lined with false Ionic columns, and four false doors mark the cardinal points, a mixture of Numidian, Egyptian and Greek styles that reflects the cosmopolitan taste of the kingdom. Inside, a long spiral corridor leads to the burial chamber, which was robbed in antiquity, and legends of hidden treasure have sent explorers into it for centuries. UNESCO listed it in 1982 together with the nearby ruins of Tipasa, which lies a short way along the coast.

The nearest towns are Tipasa, about ten kilometres away, and Hadjout and El Affroun, both bigger, so go there for fuel and food. Fuel in Algeria is inexpensive and widely available in towns, though on country roads it is wise to top up when you see a station. The best time of year is spring or autumn, when the days are warm but not harsh, and the hills are green. In the summer heat the stone glows white and the smell of dry grass and wild thyme fills the air. Stand at the foot of the tomb at dusk and the scale of it begins to sink in.

A Phoenician trading post on this stretch of the Algerian coast became a Roman colony in the first century, and by the later empire it was a prosperous town with a harbour, a forum, villas and, when the city turned Christian, several large basilicas. The remains spread along a rocky shore, among pines, wild fennel and cactus, with the dark mass of the Chenoua mountain rising behind. In the western park you walk among foundations, mosaics and column stumps with the surf rolling in beside you.

The writer Albert Camus, who grew up in Algiers, wrote one of his best-known essays about the place, Nuptials at Tipasa, in which the ruins are overgrown by wild flowers and the stones are warm to the touch. Many visitors say that nothing has changed. The site was inscribed by UNESCO in 1982 for its mixture of Punic, Roman, early Christian and Byzantine remains, and it sits only a short drive from the capital, which makes it a classic day trip for Algerians as well as foreigners.

The best time is early in the day, when the light is clear and the roads are quieter. In summer the beaches fill up, and the parking near the site can be tight. Hadjout, further inland, is a bigger market town. The air smells of salt, pine resin and the warm herbs of the maquis, and the sound of cicadas fills the afternoon. The ruins are quiet enough to hear your own footsteps on the old paving, and the sunset over the Chenoua is a very good reason to linger.
t.c6 south east area alaior@39.9,4.2:

Mahón cheese, with its protected designation of origin, is produced on farms and in dairies around the town, and the local cheesemakers will happily sell you a wedge. The town has also been a centre for footwear production for generations. There is a lively market, a pleasant plaza and a church to see if it is open.

The riding on Menorca is a pleasant, gentle kind. Roads cross the island in long, rolling lines between stone walls, fields of grass and low olive and wild olive trees, with views toward the sea from the higher spots, and traffic is light outside the summer season. Corners are mild, and the main road, which runs the length of the island, is straight and fast. The northern wind, the Tramuntana, can be strong and salty, and gusts across the open land may push a motorcycle around, so keep a firm grip. Summer brings heat and crowds to the coast, whereas spring and autumn are quiet.

Alaior has fuel stations and supermarkets, and Maó, about nine kilometres away, has everything else, including a big natural harbour and gin made from juniper, a local tradition from the days of the British garrison in the eighteenth century. The Camí de Cavalls, an old coastal path, runs around the island, and many stretches can be reached by small roads. The air smells of thyme, sea spray and warm stone, and the light is bright and clear. Take your time at the monuments, because the stones are best understood in silence.
t.necropolis puig des molins@38.9,1.4:
The hill of Puig des Molins, the hill of the windmills, rises on the edge of Ibiza Town, and under its slopes lies one of the biggest ancient cemeteries in the western Mediterranean. Over three thousand of these tombs have been found, and the city's archaeological museum, set at the top of the hill, displays the grave goods that came out of them, including pottery, jewellery, glass beads, terracotta figurines and amulets that came from as far away as Egypt.

Phoenician Ebusus was a trading post of some importance, and the island was a stop on the sea routes between the Levant, North Africa and the Iberian coast. Among the finds are terracotta figures of the goddess Tanit, who was a major deity of the Punic world, with a beautiful and slightly stern face. The dead were buried with the things they would need, so the tombs are a kind of time capsule.
