Roads cross the interior through pine woods, almond and fig groves and terraced fields, with white farmhouses and little churches, and the north coast has twisty roads with sea views. The summer traffic around the town and the airport is dense, so go early or choose spring and autumn, when the island belongs to its inhabitants again. The surface is generally good, but narrow lanes and blind bends call for care, and the wind can be strong on the coast.

Ibiza Town has about forty-eight thousand people, so fuel stations, shops and cafes are in good supply. Santa Eulària des Riu and Sant Josep have more on the other roads. The local speciality is bullit de peix, a fish stew served with rice, and flaó, a cheesecake flavoured with mint and anise. The air smells of pine, salt and herbs, and in the evening the light on the old town walls is wonderful. The museum is worth an hour, and the view from the top of the hill over the harbour is worth another.
t.poblado de sa caleta@38.9,1.3:
On a low cliff above the sea on Ibiza's south-west coast stand the foundations of some of the oldest buildings on the island. The Phoenician settlement of sa Caleta was founded around the eighth or seventh century BC, and for about a century it was a small trading post, with rectangular stone houses laid out along narrow streets, a few metres from the water. The inhabitants worked iron, a sign of their sophistication, and traded with the mainland and North Africa. Around 600 to 550 BC the village was abandoned, and its people, it seems, moved to the harbour of Ebusus, which became the main town. UNESCO included the site in its Ibiza listing of 1999.

The spot itself is wild and beautiful, with rocky coast, pines clinging to the clifftop and clear blue-green water below. A walk among the ruins takes only a short time, but the setting is special, and on a calm day you will see only a few other visitors. Not far to the south-west, the strange rock of Es Vedrà rises from the sea, an island that has attracted legends for centuries. The flat salt pans of Ses Salines, to the south-east, have been worked since Phoenician times and are home to flamingos in the cooler months.

The roads in this part of Ibiza are narrow and twisting, with plenty of short climbs, blind bends and little traffic out of season. The surface is good on the main roads, rougher on the small tracks to the coves. In July and August, the island is crowded, and every cove has its queue of cars, so spring, early summer and autumn are better. In the wind, the pines creak and the sea smells of salt and resin, and the light in the late afternoon is warm and golden.

Sant Josep de sa Talaia, the nearest village, has fuel and some shops, and the larger towns of Ibiza and Sant Antoni lie about ten to thirteen kilometres away, with everything you might need. Bring water when you visit the ruins, because there is little shade, and wear shoes with a good grip, as the rocks can be slippery. A swim after your visit is a fine way to cool off, and a plate of grilled fish at one of the beach restaurants is a decent reward.
t.palma@39.6,2.7:
Palma is a city built around a cathedral that looks like a stone cliff. La Seu, as everyone calls it, rises directly above the seafront, a Gothic mass of pale limestone begun in the early fourteenth century by King James II of Mallorca, with a huge rose window and buttresses that seem to leap toward the sea. It took centuries to build, and in the twentieth century the architect Antoni Gaudí was called in to rework the interior, hanging a great canopy above the altar. The reflection of the building in the long pond in front, at dawn, is one of the great sights of the Mediterranean.

Mallorca's capital has been a trading city since Roman times, and the old town is a maze of narrow streets, courtyards and palaces that reward aimless walking. The Castell de Bellver, a round Gothic castle on a pine-covered hill west of the city, gives a fine view of the bay. For breakfast, locals favour the ensaimada, a spiral-shaped pastry dusted with sugar, and the island is also known for sobrasada, a spreadable cured sausage, and for its almond blossom in late winter.

The great attraction for a rider is the Serra de Tramuntana, the mountain range that runs along the north-west coast and was listed by UNESCO in 2011 as a cultural landscape of terraced hillsides, ancient olive trees and stone villages. The road along it, with its endless curves, cliffs and sea views, is among the best motorcycle roads in Europe, though it can be thronged with cyclists, coaches and tourists in spring and summer. The famous road to Sa Calobra, with its hairpin turns, is a favourite, and so are the quieter roads around Valldemossa and Deià. Surface and signs are good. In the high season, the main roads can be slow, so go early, midweek, or in the shoulder months.

Palma has plenty of fuel stations, and the island's size means you are never far from one, though in the mountains they thin out. Es Molinar and the other suburbs on the east side have small harbours with seafood restaurants. In July and August, the heat and crowds are heavy, and spring and autumn are lovely. The air near the seafront smells of salt and diesel, and in the evening the cathedral glows gold. It is a fine place to begin or end a long day.
t.taroko gorge@24.2,121.6:
Taroko Gorge is the great cleft in Taiwan's eastern flank, where the Liwu river has cut through a mass of marble and schist for several million years, and where the mountains rise almost vertically from the Pacific coast to over three thousand metres. The gate at the mouth lies some twenty kilometres north of Hualien, and from there the road follows the river into a gorge so narrow in places that the walls seem to lean together overhead. The marble is grey, white and streaked, the water is a vivid turquoise, and the sound of the river echoes off the rock.

The Central Cross-Island Highway, built between 1956 and 1960, was dug by thousands of workers, many of them veterans of the civil war who had come to Taiwan with the army, and many of them died in the construction. A shrine at the entrance to the gorge, the Eternal Spring Shrine, remembers them, built on a hill over a waterfall. The road passes through tunnels cut in the rock, around the Tunnel of Nine Turns, a cliff path carved at the water's edge, and past the Swallow Grotto, where the birds nest on the cliffs. Further up, the road continues to high mountain passes at over three thousand metres, with cloud forest, cold winds and in winter the chance of snow.

The park is subject to rockfalls, landslides and earthquakes, and the road is closed from time to time. A strong earthquake struck Hualien in April 2024 and damaged parts of the gorge and its roads, and some sections were closed for repairs for a long time, so it is essential to check the current status before travelling. Typhoons between July and October can also close the route, and rain can bring sudden falls of rock. Helmets are not just a legal requirement here, and some operators insist on hard hats for walking trails.

The traffic in the gorge includes tour buses on a narrow road, so go early and ride with care. Hualien City, about twenty-one kilometres away, has fuel, food and every service, and the stations get fewer as you climb. The night market in Hualien serves excellent local snacks, including mochi and wild boar sausage, and is a pleasant way to end a day.
t.derby@-17.3,123.6:
Derby sits on a flat peninsula of mud and mangroves at the edge of King Sound, in the far north-west of Western Australia, and it is where the Gibb River Road starts. The tides here are among the biggest in the country, rising and falling about eleven metres, so the shoreline retreats for hundreds of metres twice a day and the water runs fast and brown. The town is small, with around four thousand people, and it has the dusty, relaxed air of a place that does a bit of everything: cattle, mining services, Aboriginal art and tourism.

A few kilometres out of town stands a very old boab tree known as the Prison Tree, a hollow trunk where, according to local stories, prisoners were held overnight on the way to Derby in the late nineteenth century. Historians debate details, but the tree remains a striking sight. The Mowanjum Aboriginal community nearby has an art centre that is well worth a visit, with work by Wanjina artists whose images of spirit figures stand out in the Kimberley's rock art tradition.

The Gibb River Road was built in the 1960s as a way to move cattle from the stations of the Kimberley to the port at Derby. It runs about 660 kilometres east to Wyndham and Kununurra, and for most of its length it is unsealed gravel with corrugations, creek crossings and long distances between supplies. The dry season, from about May to September, is the only sensible time to ride. In the wet, the road floods and is closed. A rider should carry plenty of water, a spare tube, tools and enough fuel for the long gaps, and tell someone the plan.

The gorges are the reward. Windjana Gorge, Tunnel Creek, Bell Gorge and Manning Gorge are all within reach, with cool water, red rock and the occasional freshwater crocodile, so swim only where signs say it is safe.
t.lake louise@51.4,-116.2:

It is a rider's delight if you are in the right frame of mind, because the speed limit is low, the road is narrow and lined with tall spruce, and there are lay-bys for wildlife. Elk, deer, bighorn sheep and the occasional black or grizzly bear all use the corridor. Please keep your distance and never stop to approach an animal. At certain times of year, part of the parkway has seasonal restrictions to protect wildlife, so check with the park before you set off.

The weather in the mountains changes fast, with snow possible any month of the year, and high passes and roads can close with little warning. Just to the west, the 101 drops down the Conejo Grade, a long, steep descent into the Oxnard Plain, with sudden views of farmland stretching to the ocean and the Channel Islands floating offshore on clear days. Trucks crawl, and the grade has a reputation for brake fires and accidents, so ride it with care and keep your distance.

South of here lie the Santa Monica Mountains, and that is where the riding becomes something special. Roads such as Potrero Road, Yerba Buena Road, Decker Canyon and Mulholland Highway wind through canyons, oak woodland and rocky ridges before dropping steeply to the Pacific Coast Highway near Malibu. These are famous motorcycle roads, technical and narrow, with blind corners, sheer drops and plenty of sport bikes on weekends. The Rock Store on Mulholland has been a gathering point for riders for decades. Speed enforcement is common and the canyons are unforgiving, so this is a place to ride well rather than fast.

The weather is usually kind: warm, dry and bright for much of the year, with cool marine air in the mornings near the coast and occasional fierce Santa Ana winds in autumn, when hot, dry gusts sweep down from the desert and raise the fire danger. Wildfires have scarred these hills many times, and after big fires the roads can be closed or damaged.

For the Pacific Coast ride toward Santa Barbara, Casa Conejo is the practical last top-up before the coastal stretch through Oxnard and Ventura. Fill the tank, get a cold drink, and enjoy the knowledge that the best views are still ahead.
t.hualien city@24.0,121.6:
Mountains and sea crowd against each other at Hualien. The city sits on a narrow coastal plain on Taiwan's east coast, with the Pacific Ocean on one side and the Central Mountain Range rising steeply to more than three thousand metres on the other, and the view from the waterfront, with the peaks looming over the town, is one of the most striking in Taiwan.

Hualien is the gateway to Taroko Gorge, a spectacular marble canyon carved by the Liwu River, with sheer walls, tunnels and suspension bridges. The region is famous for marble, quarried in the mountains and used everywhere, and for its indigenous peoples, especially the Amis and the Truku, whose culture, festivals and food are part of daily life. Hualien is also known for mochi, sticky rice cakes filled with sweet bean paste, sold in shops throughout the city, and for its night markets.

The east coast is earthquake country. In April 2024 a strong quake struck near Hualien, damaging buildings in the city and causing rockfalls and landslides in Taroko Gorge that closed roads and trails for a long time. Before riding into the mountains, check which sections of the roads and gorge are open.

For riders, Hualien is a crossroads of great routes. Highway 8, the Central Cross-Island Highway, climbs west through Taroko Gorge into the mountains, with tunnels and narrow ledges along the cliffs. Highway 11 runs south along the coast to Taitung, a wonderful ride with the ocean on one side and green hills on the other, through small villages and past beaches. Highway 9 heads north toward Su'ao along the Suhua Highway, once notorious for its narrow cliff-edge sections, now partly replaced by tunnels. Expect sudden rain, typhoons in summer and early autumn, and heavy truck traffic on the main roads.

Hualien has fuel, scooter and motorcycle shops, and food everywhere, from night markets to restaurants. Note that in Taiwan foreign riders need an international or local licence, and larger motorcycles have special rules on some roads. Qixingtan beach, just north of the city, is a curving pebble bay where you can watch the sunrise over the Pacific before starting the ride.
t.view park windsor hills@34.0,-118.4:
Up on the slopes of the Baldwin Hills, in the middle of the Los Angeles basin, View Park and Windsor Hills look out over the city in every direction: downtown's towers to the north-east, the Hollywood sign and the San Gabriels to the north, the ocean and the airport to the west. It is a leafy, quiet neighbourhood of curving streets and handsome 1920s to 1950s houses, and since the 1960s it has been one of the most affluent Black communities in the United States, sometimes called the Black Beverly Hills. Ray Charles lived here, and the area has been home to generations of doctors, judges, musicians and athletes.

A strange thing to see next door: the Inglewood Oil Field, one of the largest urban oil fields in the country, still has hundreds of pump jacks nodding away on the hills just to the north, between houses and parks. Around and above them, the Kenneth Hahn State Recreation Area and the Baldwin Hills Scenic Overlook offer trails and big views, and the overlook's steep staircase, cut into the hillside, is a favourite workout for Angelenos. At sunset, the whole basin turns gold and then glitters with lights.

Big Bear feels a world away from here. The Rim of the World Highway, Route 18, runs along the crest of the San Bernardino Mountains at around two thousand metres, with drop-offs, tight curves and views over the desert and the basin, and Big Bear Lake sits in a pine-forested valley that gets snow in winter. Coming back, you drop down to the valley and then fight your way across the freeways of the Inland Empire and Los Angeles, which can be slow, hot and stressful at rush hour. Lane splitting is legal in California, which helps, but stay alert.

Practically, everything is close: fuel, food and services along La Brea and Crenshaw, and Inglewood, home to SoFi Stadium and the Forum, right next door. Leimert Park, a few minutes away, is a centre of Black arts and culture, with galleries, music and cafés, and it is a good place to end the day with a meal.

If you have energy, ride up to the top of the hill, watch the planes line up for LAX and the sun drop into the Pacific, and know that this neighbourhood has some of the best city views in Los Angeles.
t.san clemente@33.4,-117.6:
San Clemente was designed to look Spanish. When the developer Ole Hanson founded the town in the 1920s, he wanted a Mediterranean village on the California coast, and early deeds required white walls and red tile roofs. Many of those buildings still stand, on hills that slope down to the Pacific, and the town has kept a relaxed, sunny feel, with a long wooden pier, surf shops and cafés.

It also has a presidential past. Richard Nixon bought a house on the bluffs at the southern edge of town in 1969, La Casa Pacifica, which became known as the Western White House, and he hosted world leaders there and returned to it after he resigned in 1974. The house is private, but its location, above one of the best surf breaks in California, is well known. Trestles, at San Onofre State Beach just south of town, is a world-famous surf spot, and you will see surfers walking with boards along the beach trails.

As a fuel stop, San Clemente does the job easily, with stations right off Interstate 5, the main road between Los Angeles and San Diego. South of town lies Camp Pendleton, a huge Marine Corps base that keeps the coast undeveloped for many kilometres, and the freeway runs through open hills with the ocean on one side. North of town, the Pacific Coast Highway runs through Dana Point and Laguna Beach, with cliffs, coves and expensive houses, and it is a beautiful ride, although busy with traffic on weekends.

If you are on the way to the Angeles Crest Highway or Death Valley, you have a long day ahead. The Angeles Crest, Route 2, climbs from La Cañada Flintridge into the San Gabriel Mountains, with sweeping bends and big views, and it is one of the most famous motorcycle roads in California. Death Valley is much further, through the desert. Either way, fill the tank here, eat something and drink plenty of water.

The best times on this coast are the early mornings, when the light is soft and the roads are empty, and late spring, though June can bring a grey layer of fog known as June Gloom. Order a breakfast burrito, then walk out onto the pier and watch the surfers before you head inland.
t.crest@32.8,-116.9:
Do not confuse this Crest with the Angeles Crest, which lies two hundred kilometres to the north. It has about two and a half thousand people and a rural feel, despite being so close to the city.

Crest has seen fire. In 2003, the Cedar Fire, one of the largest wildfires in California history, swept through the area, destroying many homes. The community rebuilt, but the risk remains, and in dry, windy weather, especially when the Santa Ana winds blow from the desert in autumn, the hills can be dangerous. Check fire conditions before you ride here in late summer and autumn.

As a food stop, Crest itself has very little, but El Cajon, a few kilometres west, is a surprising place to eat. It is home to one of the largest Chaldean and Iraqi communities in the United States, and its main streets are lined with Middle Eastern bakeries, markets and restaurants serving kebabs, shawarma, fresh bread and sweets. A plate of grilled meat and rice, with a cup of strong tea, is a fine meal before or after a ride.

The roads around Crest are tight and twisty, with steep climbs, blind corners and narrow lanes winding between boulders and houses. La Cresta Road and the roads through Harbison Canyon and Dehesa offer short but fun rides, and they connect to the bigger mountain roads to the east, towards Alpine, Julian and the Cuyamaca Mountains, where the riding gets even better. Watch for gravel, deer and local traffic, and remember that summer temperatures in the inland valleys can be very hot.

Bostonia, about six kilometres away, is the nearest larger community, and El Cajon has fuel, shops and services. Mount Helix, a nearby hill with a large cross and an outdoor amphitheatre at the top, offers one of the best views in San Diego County, over the ocean, the city and the mountains, and it is worth a short detour at sunset.
t.home gardens@33.9,-117.5:
Home Gardens is a small unincorporated community squeezed between Corona and Riverside, on the edge of the Santa Ana River valley, and it is a place most people pass through without noticing. It has about eleven thousand people, a mix of houses, small businesses and shopping centres, and it sits close to the Route 91 freeway, one of the busiest and most congested roads in Southern California.

Corona, right next door, has a surprisingly interesting history. In the early twentieth century it was known as the lemon capital of the world, with groves of citrus covering the valley and packing houses along the railway. Its main street, Grand Boulevard, was built as a perfect circle around the town centre, and between 1913 and 1916 it hosted road races that drew famous drivers and huge crowds, with cars roaring around the circle at what were then astonishing speeds. The circle is still there, and you can ride it today, though rather more slowly.

As a fuel stop, it is easy. There are stations along the main roads and near the freeway, along with fast food, supermarkets and convenience stores. If you are heading to Idyllwild, this is a good place to fill up before the climb into the mountains, where there is less choice and prices are often higher.

The ride from here to Idyllwild takes you east through the Inland Empire and then up into the San Jacinto Mountains, either on the Pines to Palms Highway, Route 74, from Hemet, or on Route 243 from Banning. Both climb through chaparral and then into pine forest, with tight bends, steep grades and big views over the valleys and the desert. On a hot day, the temperature drops dramatically as you climb, and the smell of pine replaces the dust of the valley.

The local riding is mostly urban, with traffic, lights and freeways, but the Santa Ana River trail and the hills around Corona offer some escape. The Prado Basin, to the west, is a large flood control area with wetlands and wildlife, and Chino Hills State Park has trails and views. Fill up here, grab a cold drink and get ready for the mountains.
t.idyllwild@33.7,-116.7:
Idyllwild is a mountain village in the San Jacinto range, high above the hot desert of Palm Springs and the sprawling valleys of the Inland Empire, set among tall pines, cedars and oaks at about 1,600 metres. It has a population of a few thousand, a village centre of wooden buildings, cafés and art galleries, and the cool, clean smell of pine that greets you as soon as you arrive.

The rocks above the village are famous among climbers. Tahquitz Rock and Suicide Rock, two great granite domes, rise above the forest, and in the 1950s climbers here developed the grading system that later became the Yosemite Decimal System, still used across North America today. On a sunny weekend you will see climbers on the walls, small as ants against the granite. Behind them, the San Jacinto peak rises to over three thousand metres, and trails lead up into the wilderness.

Idyllwild also has a quirky side. For many years the town has had an honorary mayor who is a dog, a golden retriever named Max, followed by successors with the same name, and they have become local celebrities. The village is also known for its arts, with an arts academy and many galleries, and it hosts music and arts festivals in summer.

The riding is the main reason to come. The Pines to Palms Highway, Route 74, climbs from the desert near Palm Desert in a series of switchbacks, with spectacular views over the Coachella Valley, and then winds through the mountains to join Route 243, which runs north through Idyllwild and down to Banning with tight curves and steep drops. Both roads are great motorcycle roads, with good surfaces and little traffic on weekdays. Watch for gravel, deer and snow in winter, when the roads can be icy or closed.

Idyllwild has a fuel station, cafés, restaurants and shops in the village centre, and Valle Vista, about sixteen kilometres away by road, is the nearest larger community. Fire is a real risk in these mountains, and the village has been threatened several times, so check conditions in the dry season. Find a slice of pie, sit on a bench in the sun and listen to the wind in the pines.
t.joshua tree@34.1,-116.3:
The town of Joshua Tree is a scatter of low buildings, junk-art yards, cafés and rental cabins along Highway 62, with the north entrance road to the national park running south out of it into the boulders. It sits on the high desert at around 850 metres, well above the heat of Palm Springs on the other side of the mountains, and it has become a magnet for musicians, artists, climbers and people looking to get away from Los Angeles for a weekend. The vibe is part hippie, part cowboy, part art school.

Music runs deep here. The country-rock pioneer Gram Parsons spent a lot of time in these hills and died in a motel in town in 1973, and the story of what his friends did with his body afterwards, stealing it and attempting a cremation out at Cap Rock in the park, is local legend and entirely true. U2 named an album after the place in 1987, although the tree on the cover was photographed elsewhere in the desert. Today there are music festivals, small venues and studios scattered across the Morongo Basin.

Park Boulevard heads south from town into the park through the West Entrance, and within minutes you are among the strange, spiky trees that give the place its name. Joshua trees are not really trees but giant yuccas, and they grow only in the Mojave Desert. The story goes that Mormon settlers named them because their raised branches reminded them of the prophet Joshua pointing the way. Whatever the truth, they make a weird and wonderful forest.

The riding around Joshua Tree is relaxed rather than technical. Highway 62 is a busy, straight road through the desert towns, with traffic lights and strip malls, and you will want to get off it as soon as you can. The park roads are smooth and gently curving, with low speed limits and plenty of people stopping to take photos. The best seasons are spring and autumn, when the days are warm and the nights cool, and the wildflowers bloom in March and April after a wet winter.

Joshua Tree has fuel, food, motels and rental cabins, and Yucca Valley, about ten kilometres west, is larger with supermarkets and more services. Fill up before you enter the park, because there is nowhere to buy fuel inside, and the loop through to the south entrance is long.
t.joshua tree park boulevard point 2@34.0,:
Half an hour into the park, Park Boulevard winds into the heart of the boulder country, and the landscape becomes almost absurd. Piles of rounded granite rocks, some the size of houses, rise out of the desert floor among the Joshua trees, stacked and balanced as if a giant had been playing with them.

The rocks are monzogranite, which formed deep underground as molten rock cooled more than a hundred million years ago. Water seeping through cracks rounded off the corners, and when the softer material around them eroded away, the boulders were left standing in heaps. Climbers have been coming here for decades, and on a winter weekend you will see brightly clothed figures on almost every rock face, with ropes and crash pads everywhere.

Hidden Valley is a short, easy loop trail through a natural enclosure of rocks that, according to local stories, was used by cattle rustlers to hide stolen livestock in the late nineteenth century. It is a lovely walk, about a kilometre and a half, with interpretive signs and plenty of Joshua trees and junipers. Nearby, Barker Dam is a small reservoir built by ranchers, which sometimes holds water and attracts birds and bighorn sheep, and there are petroglyphs on the rocks along the trail.

The road through this section is narrow and winding, with low speed limits and lots of parked cars. It is not a place for fast riding, but the curves are gentle and the scenery is extraordinary. Watch out for people walking along the road, cars pulling out of parking areas, and the occasional desert tortoise crossing the asphalt, a protected species that you must not disturb.

Inside the park you can buy nothing at all, and water is found only at the visitor centres and a few campgrounds. Bring everything you need, and be aware that mobile phone coverage is patchy. The best light is early morning and late afternoon, when the rocks glow orange and the shadows are long. At night the sky is very dark, and the stars are spectacular.
t.joshua tree park boulevard point 3@33.9,:
Keys View is the high balcony of Joshua Tree National Park. A side road climbs south from Park Boulevard for about ten kilometres to a viewpoint on the crest of the Little San Bernardino Mountains at around 1,580 metres, and from the edge you look out over the whole of the Coachella Valley. Below you is Palm Springs and its satellite towns, beyond them the Salton Sea glittering in the haze, and across the valley Mount San Jacinto and Mount San Gorgonio rise to over 3,000 metres, often capped with snow in winter.

The view also shows the San Andreas Fault, which runs along the foot of the mountains below you. It is the boundary between the Pacific and North American plates, and from here you can trace its line across the valley floor as a series of low ridges and changes in vegetation. On a clear day it is a geology lesson laid out in front of you, though on many days the haze from Los Angeles and the valley makes the distance fade into a blue blur.

The road up to Keys View is one of the best rides in the park, with smooth asphalt, gentle curves and steady climbing through a forest of Joshua trees and junipers. The air gets cooler as you climb, and in winter there can be frost or even snow at the top. The road is a dead end, so you will have to come back the same way, but the view is worth it.

The viewpoint is the place to watch the sunset in Joshua Tree. As the sun drops behind the mountains to the west, the valley below turns gold and pink, and the lights of the towns begin to twinkle. It can be crowded, but there is a short paved trail along the ridge where you can find a quieter spot.

Keys View has a car park and toilets and that is all. The nearest fuel is in Twentynine Palms or Joshua Tree, both about thirty kilometres away by road. The wind can be strong and cold at the top, so bring an extra layer even in spring.
t.joshua tree park boulevard point 4@33.9,:
The Cholla Cactus Garden appears out of nowhere on Pinto Basin Road, a dense patch of thousands of teddy-bear cholla cacti covering a gentle slope. From a distance they look soft and fuzzy, glowing silver in the sunlight, but up close their spines are sharp, barbed and notoriously eager to attach themselves to anything that brushes past. A short loop trail winds through the garden, and the rule is simple: look, but do not touch, and watch where you put your feet.

This part of the park is a transition zone. As you ride south from the high, boulder-strewn Mojave Desert, the Joshua trees thin out and disappear, and you enter the lower, hotter Colorado Desert, which is part of the larger Sonoran Desert. The vegetation changes to creosote bush, ocotillo and palo verde, and the land opens up into wide basins and rugged mountains. The cholla garden sits right in the middle of this transition, and a little further south there is a patch of ocotillo, the spindly cacti-like plants that burst into red flowers in spring.

The road from here is a joy for riders who like space. Pinto Basin Road descends gradually through empty desert, with long straights and gentle curves, and the views stretch for kilometres in every direction. Traffic is lighter here than in the northern part of the park, and you can often ride for long stretches without seeing another vehicle. The surface is good, but watch out for sand blown across the road and for wildlife, especially jackrabbits and coyotes at dawn and dusk.

The cholla garden is most beautiful at sunrise or sunset, when the light catches the spines and makes the whole slope glow. In the middle of the day the light is harsh and the heat can be intense, especially in summer. Spring is a good time to visit, when the ocotillo is flowering and the temperatures are mild.

There are no services here, just a small car park and the trail. The nearest fuel is in Twentynine Palms to the north or in the Coachella Valley to the southwest, and both are a good distance away. Carry water, and do not linger too long in the heat.
t.joshua tree park boulevard point 5@33.7,:
Cottonwood Spring is the southern gate of Joshua Tree, and it feels like a different park. At around 900 metres, it is lower and hotter than the northern section, with a small visitor centre, a campground and a palm oasis. A short walk from the parking area leads to a grove of California fan palms and cottonwoods around a spring that has been used by people for thousands of years. The Cahuilla people camped here, and in the late nineteenth century miners and teamsters used the water for their animals and for processing gold ore. The ruins of an old arrastra, a primitive ore-crushing mill, can still be seen nearby.

The ride from the Cholla Cactus Garden to Cottonwood Spring is a long, gradual descent through the Pinto Basin, with wide views of the Eagle Mountains and the Cottonwood Mountains. The road is straight and empty, with gentle curves and a few dips, and it is a pleasant cruise. From Cottonwood Spring the road continues south for a few more kilometres to Interstate 10, the main highway between Los Angeles and Phoenix.

Lost Palms Oasis, a longer hike from Cottonwood Spring, leads to the largest grove of fan palms in the park, hidden in a rocky canyon. The round trip is about twelve kilometres and takes several hours, so it is only for those with time and proper footwear. The trail is hot and exposed, and you should carry plenty of water.

South of Interstate 10, Box Canyon Road winds through a narrow, colourful canyon toward the town of Mecca and the Salton Sea, a fun ride with tight turns and dramatic rock walls. To the east, at Chiriaco Summit, a museum remembers General George S. Patton, who trained his troops for the North African campaign in the deserts around here during World War Two.

The visitor centre has water and toilets, but the park sells nothing else, so plan your fuel carefully. The nearest stations are at Chiriaco Summit, along Interstate 10 to the east, or in the Coachella Valley towns of Indio, Coachella and Mecca to the west. In summer, the heat at this lower elevation can be extreme, often over 40 degrees, so try to ride in the morning and take breaks in the shade.
t.taiwan central cross island highway poin:
Taroko Gorge is a slot cut through marble. The Liwu river has sawn down through a block of metamorphic rock that was lifted from the sea floor as the Philippine Sea plate pushed into Asia, and the result is a canyon so narrow in places that the cliffs nearly meet overhead, their faces streaked white, grey and pale green. The road, Provincial Highway 8, follows the river through tunnels and under overhangs, and on a quiet morning, with the river roaring below and swifts darting along the walls, it is one of the great rides in Asia.

The road itself is a monument. It was built in the late 1950s, largely by retired soldiers who had come to Taiwan with the Nationalist government, working with explosives, picks and their hands on cliffs that offered almost no footing. More than two hundred of them died during construction, and the Eternal Spring Shrine, built over a spring that pours from the cliff near the gorge entrance, commemorates them. The shrine and its waterfall make a good first stop when you enter the gorge from the Hualien side.

Further in come the famous narrows. At Swallow Grotto the cliff face is pocked with holes once used by nesting swifts, and at the Tunnel of Nine Turns the road and an old footpath wind through the narrowest part of the gorge. Helmets are recommended for walkers in some sections, which tells you everything about the rockfall risk. That risk became painfully real in April 2024, when a strong earthquake off Hualien caused huge landslides in the gorge, damaged the road and closed much of the national park. Repairs and reopening have been gradual, so check the current status of the road and the trails before you ride.

When it is open, ride it slowly. Tarmac is mostly sound, but tunnels are unlit or dim, tour buses fill the road around the main stops, and fallen stones are common after rain. Typhoon season, from late summer into autumn, can close the road for days. Hualien City, about twenty-five kilometres away, has fuel and all services, and it is wise to fill up there before entering, because stations in the mountains are few and far between.

Tianxiang is the place where Taroko Gorge opens out for a moment, and where most people stop. Two rivers meet here at the upper end of the gorge, and on a small terrace above them stand a hotel, a few shops, a bus stop and a temple, with a white pagoda on the hill above, reached by a suspension bridge across the river. After the dim tunnels and narrows below, it feels like coming up for air: the cliffs step back, the sky widens, and you can hear yourself think.

For riders on the Central Cross-Island Highway this is the last real service stop before the long climb into the mountains. Beyond Tianxiang the road leaves the marble gorge behind and begins to wind upward through forest towards the high passes, with few villages and little in the way of shops. The shops at Tianxiang sell drinks, snacks and simple meals, and it is worth topping up on water here, but for fuel you need to think ahead, filling up in Hualien and checking where the next station on your route will be.

The area has a quiet history. Before the road, the Truku people, the indigenous group whose name the gorge carries, lived in villages scattered across the terraces and slopes, and their trails linked the valleys long before the Japanese colonial authorities and later the Nationalist government built roads. Some of the old paths survive as hiking trails, such as the trail to Baiyang waterfall a little further up the road, which runs through a series of tunnels to a waterfall and a curtain of water pouring from the rock.

The 2024 Hualien earthquake hit this area hard, with landslides and damage to roads and buildings, and the reopening of the highway and trails has been a step-by-step process. Check before you go, and ask locally about rockfall. When the road is open, Tianxiang is a beautiful place to spend a night, waking up to the sound of the rivers and setting off into the mountains in the early morning, before the buses arrive. The light in the gorge is softest then, and the road is yours.

At 3,275 metres, Wuling Pass is the highest point on Taiwan's road network, and getting there is a story in itself. From the lowland heat of Hualien or Puli, the road climbs through subtropical forest, then cool broadleaf woods, then forests of hemlock and fir, until at the top you are in a world of dwarf bamboo grassland, rocky peaks and thin, cold air. It is a remarkable change for an island that sits on the Tropic of Cancer, and it means that riders who left the coast in a T-shirt need every layer they packed.

The pass lies on the shoulder of Hehuanshan, a group of peaks in Taroko National Park that are among the most accessible high mountains in Taiwan. On clear days the views stretch across ridge after ridge of the Central Mountain Range, and at sunrise and sunset the light is spectacular. In winter, cold fronts occasionally bring snow, which draws crowds from the lowlands who have never seen it, and the road can be closed or require chains. Stargazing is excellent here on clear nights, with little light pollution.

Riding up is demanding and rewarding. The roads, Highway 14A from the west and the connection to the Central Cross-Island Highway from the east, are narrow and winding, with countless hairpins, steep gradients and sections that are often wet or covered in fog. Engines lose power at this altitude, and so do riders: altitude sickness is possible if you come straight up from sea level, so take it easy, drink water and rest. Weekends bring cars and tour buses, and the descent requires care with brakes.

There are no towns at the top, just a small car park, a sign and a viewpoint. The nearest services are at Cingjing, the farm and resort area on the western side, which has hotels, restaurants and fuel, and further down, Puli, about thirty-six kilometres away, which is a town of several tens of thousands with everything a rider needs. Puli is also known for its water, used for rice wine and paper making, and for its butterflies. Top up the tank down in the valley, pack a fleece and gloves, and plan to cross early in the day, before the afternoon cloud rolls in.
t.taiwan suhua highway point 1@24.6,121.9:
Su'ao is the end of the flat land. North of the town the Lanyang plain of Yilan spreads out in rice fields and fish ponds; south of it the Central Mountain Range plunges straight into the Pacific, and the road to Hualien has to cling to the cliffs. Su'ao itself is a port town with a deep natural harbour, a naval base, a cement works and a famous cold spring, and its fishing district of Nanfang'ao, just over the hill, is one of the busiest fishing harbours on Taiwan's east coast.

The cold spring is a local curiosity. Water bubbles up naturally carbonated and cool, and the town has built public pools around it where people soak in the fizzy water on hot summer days, and where a local soda and sweets are made from it. Nanfang'ao is the place to eat: the harbour market sells mackerel, swordfish, squid and many fish you will not recognise, and restaurants will cook what you buy. The harbour also has a large temple to Mazu, the goddess of the sea, with statues made of gold and jade, a measure of what the sea means to the people here.

This is where the Suhua Highway begins, Provincial Highway 9, running south along the coast. It was once notorious, a narrow road carved into the cliffs with landslides, rockfalls and heavy trucks, and it is still a dramatic ride. Since 2020, a series of long new tunnels and bridges has made the route much safer and faster, bypassing some of the worst sections, though the old road survives in places for those who want the views. Trucks carrying cement and gravel are still a major presence, so ride defensively.

Before setting off, fill up in Su'ao or Yilan, about twenty kilometres back, because services along the coast are sparse until Hualien. The weather here is wetter than in western Taiwan, with the north-east monsoon bringing rain and wind in autumn and winter, and typhoons can close the highway entirely. Check the forecast and road conditions, and leave early. The light on the Pacific in the morning is worth the early start.
t.taiwan suhua highway point 2@24.6,121.9:
Just south of Su'ao, the first serious climb of the Suhua Highway lifts you above the sea, and suddenly the scale of the coast becomes clear. Below the road, the cliffs drop straight into deep blue water; ahead, ridge after ridge of the Central Mountain Range falls into the ocean, each one cut by a gorge, each one breaking the coastline into another bay. On clear days you can see far down the coast, and on many days you see only cloud and rain.

The coast south of here was once almost cut off from the rest of Taiwan. Indigenous Atayal villages lay in the valleys inland, and the first road along the cliffs was built during the Japanese colonial era, a narrow track for carts and later for buses that became infamous for accidents. The road clings to the cliff high above the water, passing through short tunnels and galleries.

The mountains here are being pushed up by the collision of tectonic plates, and they are being torn down just as fast by rain, rivers and earthquakes. The cliffs are one of the places where you can see this most dramatically, and the viewpoints along the road look out over wave-washed boulders and fans of gravel where streams come down. t.taiwan east rift valley point 2@23.5,121:

t.taiwan east rift valley point 3@23.1,121:

t.nakusp@50.2,-117.8:

t.vernon@50.3,-119.3:

t.lakeland village@33.6,-117.3:

t.julian@33.1,-116.6:

t.rancho palos verdes@33.7,-118.4:

t.ojai@34.4,-119.2:

t.okanagan@50.4,-119.3:

t.san pedro@33.7,-118.3:

t.near castaic on the way back@34.5,-118.5:

t.near westmont@33.9,-118.3:

t.near los serranos on the way back@33.9,-:

t.taitung@22.8,121.1:

Twenty-one miles of the Pacific Coast Highway pass through Malibu, and most of them are within sight of the sea. The road squeezes between the steep brown slopes of the Santa Monica Mountains and a narrow ribbon of sand, a mix of beach houses, small plazas, surf breaks and sudden gaps with a view over the water. The town itself has about thirteen thousand people, a city of film stars and surfers, and a strong feeling of being at the edge of something. It was once a ranch owned by the Rindge family, who held off development for decades, and the land was divided only in the 1920s, after the state forced a public road through it.

The highway is famous, and for good reason, but it is not a race track. At weekends the road fills with sightseers, delivery vans, cyclists and drivers looking for a place to park, and there are speed limits, traffic lights and patrols, with fines that are not small. The coast road has had a bad record for crashes. A good plan is to go early on a weekday, when the light comes slanting over the hills and the sea is pale blue, and the road is almost clear. In late spring and early summer the morning fog, called June gloom, can sit over the shore until noon.

For something with more bends, take one of the canyon roads that climb into the mountains. Malibu Canyon Road, Decker, Latigo and Mulholland Highway all twist up through chaparral and oak, with drops, cambers and tight corners that reward a rider with some care, and with the sea sparkling far below as you climb. They are narrow, and the surface can be rough, with gravel and fallen rock, and in places there are no barriers. Fires have swept through the mountains repeatedly, including the Woolsey fire of 2018 and the Palisades fire of 2025, leaving scars on the hills and homes, so you will see burned areas and rebuilding. Check the road status in fire season and after heavy rain, when landslides can close sections.

Fuel in Malibu is among the most expensive in California, so fill up in Santa Monica or Oxnard if you can, though there are stations along the highway. For a break, a beach cafe or a fish shack near the pier serves tacos and clam chowder with a view. The Getty Villa, a museum of ancient art in a replica Roman villa, lies a few miles south and is free to enter, with booking.
